Anyone who can open a PR in a private repo "generally those with read access" can compromise them. Runner groups limit which repositories can use them. Just-in-time runners exist (not read in detail, 📖). | ✅ | [secure-use: hardening for self-hosted runners](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) | | 3.5.3 | `GITHUB_TOKEN` is a GitHub App installation token "limited to the repository that contains your workflow". It lives at most 6 hours on hosted runners. The default org or repository setting is either "permissive" (read and write for all) or "restricted" (read for `contents` and `packages`). Per-job `permissions:` narrows it. | ✅ | [github_token](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/github_token), [disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-organization-settings/disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization) | | 3.5.3b | **Repository secrets:** "Any user with write access to your repository has read access to all secrets configured in your repository". | ✅ | [secure-use](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) | | 3.5.4 | `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` "are privileged" and "may have repository write access and access to referenced secrets". They must not check out untrusted code. | ✅ | [secure-use: untrusted code checkout](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) | | 3.5.5 | **Third-party actions:** a compromised action "would have access to all secrets configured on your repository". The strongest measure is a **workflow dependency lockfile** (`.github/workflows/actions.lock`, generated by `gh actions-lock`). It "pins a commit SHA to every action … including transitive dependencies" but does not pin reusable workflows. The alternative is full-SHA pinning. There is an org policy "Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA", and locked dependencies satisfy it. | ✅ | [secure-use: third-party actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use), [workflow-dependency-lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles), [disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-organization-settings/disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization) | | 3.5.6 | **Org audit log:**
- It covers "the last 180 days", and "only owners can access" it.
- Events include `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (a deployment approval), `environment.update_protection_rule`, `repository_ruleset.create/update/destroy`, `protected_branch.policy_override`, and `org.update_actions_secret`.
- Many events carry an `actor_is_agent` field. **Its meaning is not defined** in the pages read (⚠️).
- The log can be exported as JSON or CSV, within documented "Export limits". Streaming was not researched (⚠️). | ✅ / ⚠️ (`actor_is_agent`, streaming) | [secure-use](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use), [reviewing-the-audit-log-for-your-organization](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/reviewing-the-audit-log-for-your-organization), [audit-log-events](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/audit-log-events-for-your-organization) | ### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design) These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts: 1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.** - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval is per deployment job and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6). - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by: - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, an empty bypass list (3.2.2–3.2.4); - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3). - **Prerequisite on both plans: the branch rule alone does not mean "only merged, approved code reaches prod".** Every workflow on `main` passes a "main only" rule, whatever its trigger (3.4.5c). So all of the following must also hold: - only reviewed deploy workflows may reference `production`, enforced by CODEOWNERS on `.github/workflows` and a CI check; - deploy workflows take no ref or SHA input, and deploy the commit they run on; - no `production` job runs on `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`. A `schedule` deploy of the current `main` commit is acceptable only if it deploys that commit and takes no input; - preferably, the `sub` claim is pinned to the reusable deploy workflow (`job_workflow_ref`, 3.4.5). Under these conditions, merge approval equals deploy approval on Team. - **Admins remain a gap.** Admins and holders of "edit repository rules" can edit rulesets, environments and the OIDC `sub` customisation. This is mostly logged, not prevented (3.1.4, 3.2.2, 3.4.5). So: few admins, periodic access review, and alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`, `environment.remove_protection_rule`, `environment.delete` and `protected_branch.policy_override`. - **UI changes to the branch policy may not be audited** (⚠️, 3.1.4). A deleted `production` environment is likely recreated without protection by the next workflow that references it. The deletion itself is logged (⚠️ inference, 3.1.4). So a scheduled job should also compare the live environment configuration with the expected one, as drift detection (⚠️: the REST endpoint was not researched). - **GĐ-5 holds only on Enterprise.** It should go back to the framing as a correction and an open question for Papaya. 2. **OIDC trust must pin the repository, the gate and, where possible, the workflow** (3.4.2–3.4.5c): - **AWS:** prod roles trust only `repo:/:environment:production`, in the repo's `sub` format (3.4.4). Ideally a customised `sub` includes `job_workflow_ref`, because AWS cannot test other claims (3.4.5). - **GCP:** the attribute condition must restrict to the GitHub organization (required by Google). It can also test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` and `event_name` directly (3.4.5b). - **Non-prod:** roles trust a separate environment. - **Secrets:** prod credentials never live in repository secrets, because anyone with write access can read those (3.5.3b). This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5). 3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals or a custom check whose source app is pinned. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays **off** (3.3.3). 4. **CI agents and policy files:** on standard GitHub-hosted runners, an agent with shell access has root, so Claude Code managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the Topic 1 question). The real limits for a CI agent are: - the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3); - **no** `environment: production` in any agent workflow, so it gets no prod OIDC trust (3.4.5c); - the base-branch config restore in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9). Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring persistence risks (3.5.2). 5. **Supply chain of CI itself:** - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5). - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid lines fail silently (3.2.7). - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4). 6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA evidence needs longer, so it must be exported periodically (JSON or CSV, within the export limits, ✅) or streamed (⚠️ not researched; may be Enterprise-only). ### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3) #### Giả định của owner (2026-11-08) **These are design assumptions set by the repo owner, not facts about Papaya.** The owner has no access to Papaya's systems. Recorded verbatim, as written by the owner in the session of 2026-11-08: > 1. Gói GitHub: giả định Papaya dùng gói Team (không phải Enterprise). > 2. Format `sub` của OIDC: giả định repo dùng format mới (có ID). Mình không biết ngày tạo repo thật của Papaya. > 3. Claude GitHub App: mình chưa biết nó ghi tác giả PR và commit thế nào. Giả định xấu nhất: tác giả PR là app, người gọi agent vẫn tự duyệt được. Thiết kế không được dựa vào hành vi mặc định của app. > 4. Merge queue : Giả định là có sử dụng merge queue, thiết kế cần chạy được với merge queue thì chỉ ghi rõ cần thêm gì, đừng đổi giả định. **Owner decision on the A1/A4 conflict (2026-11-08), verbatim:** > Giữ Team và bỏ merge queue. So the design assumes **Team and no merge queue**. A4 is superseded. Its row below is kept only as a reference for a possible later move to Enterprise Cloud; the design does not use it. **Consequences for the design.** These are my inferences from 3.1–3.6, unless a source is given. The "cheap to cover the other case" lines do not change the assumptions. | Assumption | Consequence for the design | Cheap to cover the other case | |---|---|---| | A1 — GitHub **Team** | Environment approval gates are unavailable on the private monorepo (3.1.2). **The approval gate is the PR merge to `main`, enforced by rulesets** (3.2.1–3.2.4): PR required, approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, approval after the last push, and an empty bypass list. The `production` environment is restricted to `main` (3.1.3). All the prerequisites in 3.6 #1 apply: only reviewed deploy workflows reference `production`, deploys take no ref input, and no privileged triggers are used. Admin edits are logged, not prevented. Drift detection is needed (3.1.4, 3.6 #1). | Create the `production` environment now, with the branch restriction. If Papaya moves to Enterprise Cloud, add required reviewers, prevent self-review, and disallow admin bypass on that environment. This is a settings change only; the workflows and the OIDC trust stay the same (inference). | | A2 — immutable `sub` (with IDs) | AWS and GCP trust conditions must match `repo:@/@:environment:production` (inference from the documented `ref` examples), with placeholders in `examples/` (3.4.4). If the `sub` is customised with `job_workflow_ref` (3.4.5), the IDs stay in the `repo` segment and cannot be removed (3.4.4, oidc reference). | The org or repo can **opt in** to immutable subject claims (3.4.4). Opting in makes A2 true regardless of the repo's creation date. Accepting the old format as well would bring back the namespace-recycling risk, so it is not recommended. | | A3 — worst case: the app is the PR author, and the person who triggered the agent can approve | The built-in "authors cannot approve" rule cannot be relied on (3.3.1, 3.3.4). Protected branches need **2 approvals**, at least on paths an agent can change, **or** a required status check whose **expected source app is pinned** (3.2.5, 3.3.4). The check fails when the approver is the person who triggered the agent run. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays off (3.3.3), but that setting covers only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, not the Claude App's own token. **Worst case also covers the app approving:** whether an approval from a GitHub App counts toward required approvals is open (⚠️; only Copilot's is documented not to count, 3.3.1). The pinned check must therefore confirm **at least one approval from a human other than the person who triggered the agent**, rather than count approvals. Where configurable, the app gets no permission to approve PRs. Agent workflows never reference `production` (3.6 #4). | These rules still hold, and cost little, if the app turns out to attribute PRs to the human. | | A4 — merge queue in use (**superseded 2026-11-08: no merge queue**; reference only) | Workflows that report required checks **must also trigger on `merge_group`**: "You **must** use the `merge_group` event to trigger your GitHub Actions workflow when a pull request is added to a merge queue" ([managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue), ✅). `merge_group` runs carry the merge-group ref (3.4.5c), so a `production` environment restricted to `main` does not serve them. That is the intended result, **provided the environment uses "Selected branches" with exactly `main`**: queue branches are named `gh-readonly-queue/main/…`, and "Protected branches only" or a broad pattern may behave differently (⚠️). Queue runs are CI only, and the deploy runs on `main` after the queue merges. PRs must pass the required protections before a user "can add the pull request to the queue" (same page, ✅). **What must be added for the gate:**
- (a) the A3 self-approval check, and every gate check, must also run on `merge_group` and evaluate **each PR in the group**. This means mapping the group back to its PRs and approvers (⚠️ design).
- (b) enable "Only merge non-failing pull requests". When it is off, "Pull requests that have failed required checks can be added to a group as long as the last pull request in the group has passed" (same page, ✅). That would let a PR that failed the self-approval check through.
- (c) turn on the "Require merge queue" setting. The queue page says it is "configured under branch protection rules or rulesets" ([about-protected-branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches), [managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue), ✅).
**Audit evidence:** with a queue, the queue performs the merge, so the "merged by" actor may not be the approver (⚠️ not verified). Evidence for Compliance should come from the review approvals and the add-to-queue event. ⚠️ Also not verified: that the queue's merge to `main` triggers `push` workflows as a normal merge does. | Adding `merge_group` triggers does no harm in a repo without a queue. | **Conflict between A1 and A4. Resolved 2026-11-08 by the owner: keep Team, drop the merge queue.** - The merge queue page says: "Pull request merge queues are available in any public repository owned by an organization, or in private repositories owned by organizations using GitHub Enterprise Cloud" (plan banner of [managing-a-merge-queue](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-a-merge-queue), ✅). - So on the **Team** plan, a **private** monorepo cannot use a merge queue. A1 and A4 cannot both hold. - The design above works under either one, because nothing in it depends on the queue. The only difference is whether `merge_group` triggers are needed. **Questions to ask Papaya if there is a chance** (the open items below remain open; the owner's assumptions do not answer them): - [ ] ⚠️ **Papaya's GitHub plan** (Team vs Enterprise Cloud). It decides 3.6 #1. *Design assumption: Team (A1); GĐ-5 updated accordingly on 2026-11-08.* - [ ] ⚠️ On Team private repos, can admins bypass the environment branch restriction at run time, and is a UI change to the branch policy audited (3.1.4)? Are org-level rulesets available on Team (3.2.1, the docs contradict each other)? - [ ] ⚠️ Which plans allow OIDC subject customisation (3.4.5), and whether Papaya's monorepo uses the old or the immutable `sub` format (3.4.4). *Design assumption: immutable (A2).* - [ ] ⚠️ Audit-log streaming and its plan; meaning of `actor_is_agent` (3.5.6). - [ ] ⚠️ How the Claude GitHub App attributes PRs and commits, whether the triggering human is recorded anywhere usable for a self-approval check, and whether an approval from a GitHub App counts toward required approvals (Copilot's does not, 3.3.1) (3.3.4). *Design assumption: worst case (A3).* - [ ] ⚠️ Does Papaya use a merge queue? (`merge_group` runs carry the merge-group ref, 3.4.5c.) *Design assumption: no merge queue (owner decision 2026-11-08, A4 superseded).* - [ ] ⚠️ Does sudo exist on single-CPU hosted runners (3.5.1)?

The same goes for the Serverless Framework major version and 945 subscription. Each row says when it depends on one of these. 946 947 ### 4.1 Pulumi: preview and up in CI 948 949 | # | Finding | Marker | Source | 950 |---|---|---|---| 951 | 4.1.1 | `pulumi preview` flags relevant to CI: `--diff`, `--json`, `--expect-no-changes` ("Return an error if any changes are proposed"), `--policy-pack`, `--refresh`, `--target`, and `--save-plan` (marked **[PREVIEW]**). `--show-secrets` defaults to false; "if used with `--save-plan` the secrets will also be shown in the plan file". | ✅ | [pulumi preview](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_preview/) | 952 | 4.1.2 | `pulumi up` flags: `--yes` ("Automatically approve and perform the update after previewing it"), `--skip-preview`, `--plan ` (**[EXPERIMENTAL]**: "will not perform operations that exceed its plan"), `--strict` (**[EXPERIMENTAL]**: generate a plan during preview and constrain the update to it), and `--expect-no-changes`, where "This check happens after the update is applied". | ✅ | [pulumi up](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_up/) | 953 | 4.1.3 | **Update plans:** "`pulumi preview --save-plan=plan.json`" then "`pulumi up --plan=plan.json`" constrains the update "to allow only the changes described in the plan". The docs say this "may be useful in organizations with strict approval processes".
Limits:
- Values unknown at preview time are recorded as `unknown`.
- Resources created inside an `apply` are not recorded, which causes an error at update time.
- Providers with unknown inputs are not fully diffed.
- The docs say the plan is "not as strong a guarantee as to what the program will do".
- The plan file format "is currently experimental and subject to change". | ✅ | [Update plans](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/operations/stack-management/update-plans/) | 954 | 4.1.4 | Pulumi's GitHub Actions guide uses `pulumi/actions` (`command: preview` on `pull_request`, `up` on push), with optional PR comments. It recommends **OIDC token exchange** through `pulumi/auth-actions` ("no stored secret") over a stored `PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN`. Cloud credentials come either from Pulumi ESC or directly from cloud OIDC, for example `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`. The guide assumes Pulumi Cloud, but "Pulumi Cloud isn't required to run Pulumi in CI/CD". The guide calls ESC "the recommended way to provide cloud credentials". For deployments it advises "a shared group *without* `cancel-in-progress`" because "canceling a deployment mid-run can leave infrastructure half-applied". | ✅ | [GitHub Actions](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/operations/continuous-delivery/github-actions/) | 955 | 4.1.5 | **Pulumi Cloud OIDC trust for GitHub:**
- Organization tokens are available on the Essentials, Pro and Enterprise editions.
- Team tokens are available on Pro and Enterprise. Personal tokens also exist.
- The example subject is `repo:/:*`. **Inference:** that is the old `sub` format (3.4.4) with a wildcard, which matches any branch, PR or environment.
- Whether the Pulumi policy can pin `environment:production` was not checked (⚠️).
- Setting it up requires being "an admin of your Pulumi organization". | ✅ / ⚠️ | [OIDC: GitHub](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/administration/guides/oidc-issuers/github/) | 956 957 ### 4.2 Pulumi: policy as code ("CrossGuard") 958 959 | # | Finding | Marker | Source | 960 |---|---|---|---| 961 | 4.2.1 | **Naming:** the current docs call the product **"Pulumi Policies"**. "CrossGuard" does not appear in any Pulumi page downloaded (`grep -c -i crossguard` = 0). The old URL `https://www.pulumi.com/docs/using-pulumi/crossguard/` redirects (HTTP 200) to the policy-as-code page (**local check**, `curl -sIL`). So "CrossGuard" is the old name of Pulumi Policies. | ✅ | [Policy as code](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/discovery-governance/concepts/policy-as-code/) | 962 | 4.2.2 | Policies are written in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python or OPA Rego. They run as analyzer plugins during `pulumi preview` and `pulumi up`, "before anything changes in your cloud provider", and "a violation of a mandatory policy stops the deployment". The enforcement levels are `advisory`, `mandatory`, `remediate` and `disabled`. | ✅ | [Policy as code](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/discovery-governance/concepts/policy-as-code/), [Policy packs](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/discovery-governance/concepts/policy-as-code/policy-packs/) | 963 | 4.2.3 | **Two ways to enforce:**
- **Open source, local:** the job runs `--policy-pack `. This works "with any backend, including the self-managed backend". The pack must be on disk where Pulumi runs.
- **Pulumi Cloud** (Essentials, Pro and Enterprise): policy groups apply packs to stacks "without passing `--policy-pack` on each command", and the CLI downloads them automatically. Audit policies over discovered resources need Pulumi Cloud. | ✅ | [Policy as code](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/discovery-governance/concepts/policy-as-code/) | 964 | 4.2.4 | **Inference:**
- **Local enforcement:** the policy flag lives in the CI workflow. A PR that edits the workflow can drop it, so it is only as strong as CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8).
- **PR preview:** policy packs run on "the machine that runs Pulumi", together with the PR's code. So in a PR preview a policy result is advice. The **enforcing** run is `up` on `main`.

- **Scheduled (Pulumi Cloud Deployments):** available on the **Pro and Enterprise** editions. It needs the stack's "deployment settings", so Pulumi Cloud must hold credentials for the target. Optional **auto-remediation** "runs `pulumi up --refresh`". That is an unreviewed prod change.
- **From the CLI:** `pulumi refresh --preview-only` ("Only show a preview of the refresh"), which a job on any backend can run on a schedule (inference).
- The CLI drift guide (`/docs/iac/operations/stack-management/drift/`) was **not read** (⚠️). | ✅ / ⚠️ | [Drift detection and remediation](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/deployments/concepts/drift/), [pulumi refresh](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_refresh/) | 972 | 4.3.3 | **Backends:** Pulumi Cloud, the default, or **DIY**: S3, Azure Blob, GCS, an S3-compatible store, PostgreSQL or local disk. "DIY backends include built-in state locking and history tracking". The S3 backend needs `s3:ListBucket`, `GetObject`, `PutObject` and `DeleteObject` under `.pulumi/` "across the full stack lifecycle", including `pulumi preview`. PR code can therefore apply to non-prod, which is acceptable because non-prod holds no real data (GĐ-14); - **prod deploy:** trusts `environment:production` only; - **prod drift check:** a separate read role trusted only from a dedicated `drift` environment restricted to `main`. The change persists after the next deploy (4.4.4). In prod, deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` **and** `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` to every principal except the CloudFormation `deploymentRole`. - This works only if `deploymentRole` is set. So keeping state-changing commands (`state …`, `import`, `destroy`, `stack rm`) out of prod runs is enforced only by the workflow allowlist plus CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8). This avoids a long-lived GitHub secret (4.4.8, 3.5.3b). ### 4.7 Open items (Topic 4) - [ ] ⚠️ Papaya's Pulumi backend (Pulumi Cloud vs DIY S3) and edition; Serverless version

## Topic 5 — Compliance: ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A, HIPAA Security Rule, regional law, suppliers Accessed 2026-11-08. Scope: the controls that bear on **production change, access control, logging and suppliers**. PHI definitions, BAA conditions and the Anthropic BAA are already in 1.11 and are not repeated here. Sources and how they were read: - **HIPAA Security Rule:** 45 CFR 164.304, 164.306, 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314, 164.316, read as of 2026-11-01 through the official eCFR API (**local check**, HTTP 200). HHS.gov still returns 403 (see 1.11). - **Proposed Security Rule changes:** Federal Register API, document 2024-30983, plus its full text (**local check**, HTTP 200). - **Vietnam:** Law 91/2025/QH15 and Decree 356/2025/NĐ-CP, read as the PDFs published in the official gazette (*Công báo*, congbaocdn.chinhphu.vn). The text was extracted locally with `pypdf` (**local check**). The Ministry of Justice database (vbpl.moj.gov.vn) did not resolve (DNS), and vbpl.vn returned 403. - **Google Cloud:** the HIPAA compliance page and the Agent Platform release notes, raw HTML (**local check**, HTTP 200). - **Anthropic:** `hipaa-setup` (raw `.md`), `settings-hipaa.json` and `README-hipaa.md` from the official `anthropics/claude-code` repository (**local check**: `json.tool` validates the file). Also two Claude Help Center articles, read with WebFetch. - **GitHub and AWS:** compliance pages (**local check**, HTTP 200). **Source gap: the ISO/IEC 27001 text is not available to me.** - The standard is sold by ISO. `iso.org/standard/27001` returned **HTTP 403** to curl and to WebFetch (**local check**). - NIST publishes a crosswalk "800-53 Rev. 5 to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (OLIR)", linked from the [SP 800-53 Rev. 5 page](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final). Its catalog page ([referenceId=155](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/olir/informative-reference-catalog/details?referenceId=155)) renders only in a browser, and I could not reach its data with curl (**local check**). - The AWS Audit Manager framework list has only "ISO/IEC 27001:2013 Annex A" (**local check**). - **Therefore every ISO clause number, Annex A control number and control title in 5.1 is ⚠️ (recalled, not read).** They must be checked against Papaya's licensed copy of the standard, or the NIST crosswalk opened in a browser, before they go into `docs/`. ### 5.1 ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Annex A controls relevant to the agent workflow | # | Finding | Marker | Source | |---|---|---|---| | 5.1.1 | **The 2022 edition is the current certification basis.** AWS describes "ISO/IEC 27001:2022" as "a security management standard that specifies security management best practices and comprehensive security controls following the ISO/IEC 27002 best practice guidance". Both require unique identity, audit controls, integrity and records. So the design should present the Compliance rule as Papaya's chosen way to meet 8.32 / 5.3 and 164.312(a)(2)(i) / (b) / (c). The record chain in 5.6 is what proves it to an auditor. 2. **Retention value: at least 6 years for approval and change records.** 164.316(b)(2)(i) requires 6-year retention of required documentation (5.2.9). Whether raw audit logs themselves must be kept 6 years is interpretation (⚠️). Topic 2 already plans an organization trail to a log-archive account with an explicit retention decision (2.9); this sets the value for approval and change records. **New item:** the GitHub org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6), so the GitHub side needs its own export. 3. **Emergency access (⚠️ mapping).** HIPAA requires a documented procedure for obtaining ePHI during an emergency (5.2.6). It does not speak about production changes. A break-glass path to prod is one common way to support it, and the agreed "incident approvals within 15 min, 24/7" is Papaya's policy for emergency changes. Either way, the emergency path must leave the same evidence as the normal one. 4. **Cross-border transfer in the Vietnam example (⚠️ inference).** A Claude session is a platform outside Vietnam (5.4.5). If it processed personal data collected in Vietnam, that would be a cross-border transfer. If Papaya already moves Vietnamese personal data to foreign cloud, it already holds (or owes) a transfer impact assessment, and agent data flows would be an **update** to it (Art. 20(3), Art. 22), not a new duty. Two cautions: - "Infrastructure metadata" is not automatically free of personal data: CloudTrail events, git history and session transcripts contain **employee** names and emails. Two exemptions concern employee data: Law Art. 20(6)(b) (storing own employees' data on cloud) and Decree Art. 17(3)(d) (cross-border HR management). Whether sending employee identities in logs to a model provider falls under either is ⚠️. - Extending the owner's PHI decision (1.9) from PHI to **all customer personal data** (including basic data such as ID numbers, 5.4.3) is a scope change. It is a question for the owner, not a settled decision (5.8). **Owner decided 2026-11-08: not extended (5.8).** 5. **Sensitive data needs written access rules** (Decree Art. 4(2), 5.4.3). The Topic 2 design of no data-plane access for agent identities (2.9; PHI paths in 1.11.4) is the matching control, and its SCP/IAM text is the written rule. 6. **The NPRM shows where the requirements are heading** (5.3.2): MFA on all relevant ePHI systems and for privilege changes, real-time monitoring and recording of activity, yearly vendor verification and an asset inventory. MFA through Identity Center and a supplier register are cheap. Real-time monitoring of **all** activity is not: CloudTrail data events cover only the RDS Data API, not SQL sent over database connections (⚠️ inference, 2.7.1). The design should label these as forward-looking, not as current requirements. 7. **Supplier register entries are concrete** (5.5.1–5.5.3): Anthropic and GitHub certificates are self-service for org owners or via the Trust Portal. The GCP BAA covers Agent Platform generative AI but **not Firebase**, so Firebase Hosting must stay PHI-free (consistent with a static front end, ⚠️ not verified for Papaya). 8. **Team-plan limits remain visible.** Tenant Restrictions (5.5.6) is available to Enterprise plans and Console organizations, so a Team org cannot use it to block claude.ai sign-ins to other organizations (⚠️ inference). Stopping use of personal accounts on corporate code then depends on network and device controls (MDM is unknown, 1.9). `settings-hipaa.json` (5.5.4) is still a good **template** for Team managed settings, key by key, subject to Topic 1's plan notes. The README says it applies "whether or not the HIPAA configuration is in effect", and that the same keys must also go into server-managed settings if the org uses them (5.5.4). 9. **Risk-register input from the README** (5.5.5, 5.5.5b): the laptops' managed file does not reach the Claude Code GitHub Action, so CI needs its own runner-side file (1.7.10 b), which can be tampered with on hosted runners (3.5.1). Injected instructions are limited only by the sandbox network allowlist, and in auto mode a classifier, not a person, approves actions. ### 5.8 Open items (Topic 5) #### Quyết định của owner (2026-11-08) - Question: extend "no PHI to the agent" to "no customer personal data to the agent" (5.7 #4)? Agent data flows would be an update. So the production boundary must not rest on the model or the classifier: - **Outside incidents:** no standing prod write for humans or agents (2.9 #2). Prod changes go only through CI with a human approval in GitHub (Topics 3–4). This is OWASP's "downstream" approval (6.1.4). - **Inside a JIT window:** on the laptop the agent can use the grant, because it is indistinguishable from the engineer (2.9 #1, residual risk). This is exactly when the engineer is reading logs and alerts, which are untrusted input (#8). So during incidents untrusted input and prod write **overlap**. The compensating control is an owner decision, for example "no agent session in the shell that holds the JIT grant", or the agent only proposes commands that the human runs (⚠️ design). - The classifier, the probe and the sandbox **reduce frequency**; IAM and the CI gate **limit impact**. 2. **Separate reading untrusted content from holding power (⚠️ design).** This follows NIST's "multiple LLMs with different permissions" (6.1.2). On a laptop there is no Claude Code or AWS mechanism that separates credentials per session (2.9 #1). Separation therefore means a different OS user, container, VM or CI runner with **its own** credentials. Examples: a PR-review agent in CI with read-only tokens, and a sandboxed dev container without the engineer's SSO cache. 3. **Auto mode is on by default, so Papaya must decide explicitly** (6.3.2). Its default block list **overlaps with** the Compliance position (prod deploys, IAM grants, merging unapproved PRs, 6.3.3). It is not a named human, and it allows pushing to the default branch by default. That is safe only if rulesets require an approved PR on `main` (3.6). The measured miss rates are per risk: - 17% on 52 real overeager actions; - 5.7% on 1,000 synthetic exfiltration attempts; - no published rate for the injection probe. Both rates date from 2026-03-25, before the v2.1.283 default (6.3.5). Options for the design: - (a) Disable it org-wide with `disableAutoMode`. - (b) Set `permissions.defaultMode` in managed settings so sessions start in Manual. People "can still switch to auto mode" ([permission-modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes)). - (c) Allow it only in environments whose credentials are non-prod. No setting ties auto mode to credentials, so this needs a separate machine, container or profile (#2, ⚠️). With (b) and (c), `autoMode.environment` must not list PHI-holding buckets as trusted, because "Sending data to the trusted domains, buckets, and services you list" is allowed by default. The trade-off is a measured miss rate against approval fatigue. Anthropic itself says that for someone "manually approving every action carefully, it's arguably a regression". So the owner decides (6.6). My unverified expectation (⚠️) is that (a) increases prompt fatigue. 4. **Version floor and two policy channels.** The advisory record (6.3.9) makes a minimum client version a security control. GHSA-gfvf (6.3.10) affected **Team** server-managed settings and not endpoint-managed files. So: - set `requiredMinimumVersion` at or above 2.1.260 (and above later fixes). Note it does not end a running session and fails open on an invalid value (1.1.13). Clients on 2.1.283 or later start in auto mode anyway; a floor there makes that universal unless #3 changes it; - deliver the key settings **both** server-managed and as an endpoint file where MDM exists (1.9: MDM unknown). A local admin can still edit the endpoint file (1.1.8). 5. **Repository-controlled configuration is a recurring bug class** (6.2.1, 6.3.9). - Put `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`, `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc` and `.github/` under CODEOWNERS. This extends 3.2.8, which covers `.github/workflows` only. - In CI, run the agent only with base-branch configuration (6.3.8). Remember that `package.json`, `Makefile`, lockfiles, `.npmrc` and `bunfig.toml` still come from the PR head. So keep hook, `statusLine` and `apiKeyHelper` commands self-contained. - In `-p`/CI sessions, project `.mcp.json` servers load without a prompt (6.2.1). The CI configuration should therefore fix the MCP set itself (1.3). - `CLAUDE.md` is also classifier input (6.3.4), so a PR that edits it changes what the classifier treats as intent (⚠️ inference). 6. **Exfiltration goes through allowed channels.** Allowing `github.com` wholesale is a documented path (6.3.7). The README says injected content can move data "through the developer's own shell and Git", limited only by the network allowlist (5.5.5). Other outbound channels are PR, issue, Linear and Slack posts through MCP. Controls: - a narrow egress allowlist, or a TLS-inspecting proxy for the strongest guarantee (6.3.7); - MCP write tools for chat and tickets only where needed. The Engineering cost is the workflows that break. 7. **Supply chain is an agent risk, not only a CI risk.** Agents run installs (6.2.6), and auto mode allows "Installing dependencies declared in your lock files or manifests" by default (6.3.3). A lockfile does not stop a locked malicious version from running `postinstall`. Candidate controls (⚠️): - `--ignore-scripts` where workable, and an internal registry or mirror; - least-privilege, short-lived CI tokens (Topic 3). The Amazon Q release was built with a mis-scoped token; the payload was "unsuccessful in executing due to a syntax error" (6.2.7); - pinned plugins from Papaya's private marketplace, with a client version that includes the pin fix (2.1.179). 8. **Logs and tickets are untrusted input** (6.2.5, ⚠️). Text from customer-facing systems can carry instructions when it reaches CloudWatch, Linear or Slack. Papaya is multi-tenant, so a session that reads one insurer's logs and can write to shared places (PRs, tickets, chat) is also a cross-tenant leak path (⚠️). This falls under #2. 9. **Persistence and transcripts.** An injection that writes to agent configuration or memory outlives the session (GHSA-ff64, 6.3.9). The controls differ per target (6.3.11): - `.claude/settings.json` (hooks) is a protected path: prompted in Manual, sent to the classifier in auto mode, and never classifier-approved with `--restricted`; - the repo's `CLAUDE.md` is not protected. Only CODEOWNERS and PR review control it (#5); - **auto memory** (`~/.claude/projects//memory/`) is exempt from protected paths unless the session runs with `--restricted`, and it lives outside the repo, so CODEOWNERS cannot see it (⚠️ gap; see 6.6); - session transcripts under `~/.claude/projects/` hold tool output, which is a store for secrets and data (1.11.4). Auto mode blocks "Printing a live credential or token into the transcript" (permission-modes block list), but tool output that already contains data is still stored. 10. **Attribution depends on where the agent runs** (3.3.1, 3.3.4). - **Laptop:** agent commits and PR comments carry the engineer's identity; MCP posts (Slack, Linear) probably do too, depending on how each server authenticates (⚠️). This is the git-side twin of 2.9 #1. GitHub already blocks the engineer from approving that PR (3.3.1). - **`claude-code-action` / GitHub App:** if the app opens the PR, the author is the app, and the engineer who triggered it is **not** blocked from approving it. One approval could then mean zero independent reviewers. The mitigations are in 3.3.4. 11. **Open-ended tools are a deliberate trade-off.** OWASP says to "Avoid open-ended extensions (e.g. run a shell command, fetch a URL)" (6.1.4). Claude Code's Bash and WebFetch are exactly that. Keeping them is the Engineering value; the sandbox, egress limits and the CI boundary are the price paid for keeping them. 12. **Test the controls.** OWASP lists adversarial testing (6.1.1), and NIST names AgentDojo (6.1.5). The rollout should include a planted-injection exercise against the real configuration, for example a PR comment or a log line that asks the agent to exfiltrate data or deploy. ### 6.6 Open items (Topic 6) #### Quyết định của owner (2026-11-08) Recorded as the owner wrote them (Vietnamese, verbatim). # Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya

> Status: draft v1, for owner review · Updated: 2026-11-09
> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Every layer states what it costs engineers and
> what it gives Compliance.

## How to read this

The framework has eight layers. Each layer has three parts:

- **Principle**: the rule, independent of any tool. It still holds if a tool changes.
- **On Papaya's stack**: how the rule is applied with Pulumi, Serverless Framework, GitHub
  Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s and Claude Code.
- **Audit evidence**: the records the layer produces, so an auditor can test it without asking
  anyone.

Markers (see `CLAUDE.md` Rule 1):

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented behaviour. R*x.y* is the row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes the official page and links it. |
| ✅ | Checked locally in this repository. |
| ⚠️ | Assumption, inference or open question. Not verified. |
| [design] | A mechanism I propose. It is built from documented parts, but nobody has tested it. Treat it as ⚠️. |

Other references: **GĐ-n** = owner-confirmed assumption n in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4;
**S-n** = success criterion n (same file, §5); **P-n / A-n** = problems (same file, §1);
**D1–D3** = owner decisions in `work/02-research.md` 6.6; **Options §n** = `work/03-options.md`.

---

## 1. The decision in one page

**The conflict is narrow.** Engineering and Compliance disagree only about *writes to
production*. Reading metadata and everything in non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence
(framing §3.1). Reading real customer data is a separate question (layer 6).

**Chosen approach: "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):

1. **Every production change is a pull request**, approved by a named human who is not the author,
   and applied by the CI pipeline. This holds during incidents too ("IaC first").
2. **A narrow fallback**: when the PR path cannot be used (the operation is not expressible in IaC,
   or GitHub Actions is down), a human gets a short, approved just-in-time (JIT) permission. The
   approver approves an exact list of commands. A human runs them in a terminal without an agent.
   Afterwards a job reconciles CloudTrail with the list, and a PR codifies the change.
3. **The agent never holds production write access**, on a laptop or in CI.

What each side gets:

| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
|---|---|
| A free loop in non-prod: the agent reads, changes and deploys without approval (GĐ-14 makes this safe). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced by GitHub rulesets and AWS IAM, which the agent cannot edit. |
| Read-only prod metadata for the agent (config, metrics, redacted logs). | No standing prod write for any human or agent (S1); no long-lived keys in CI (S2). |
| Self-service: open a PR, get one approval, ship the same day (S4: wait ≤ 1 h in working hours). | One evidence chain per change, kept ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9, R5.7 #2). |
| An incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min 24/7 (S7), decision-to-apply ≤ 30 min (Options §9 Q3). | Agent-side controls (managed settings, catalogue) as a second layer, not as the control of record. |

**Where the design does not fully meet Compliance's sentence (stated openly):**

- **The JIT fallback meets it only partly.** The approver approves a command list, not an applied
  change, and "the human, not the agent, ran it" is a process rule (Options §5.1). The owner
  accepted this (Options §9 Q2). It is measured (layer 7).
- **On the GitHub Team plan nobody sees the prod diff before apply.** The reviewer sees the code diff
  and a non-prod preview (📖 R4.6 #1, R3.1.2). The deploy job stops on risky prod diffs and asks for a
  second approval [design].

**Cross-cutting rules** (from the owner's balance principle, `work/02-research.md` 6.8):

1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Agent-side controls lower how often things go wrong;
   they do not decide what is possible (📖 R1.1.7, R1.8 #1).
2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds.** No source claims a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
   Design so that a hijacked agent can do little.
3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small.** If the safe path is slower than the
   shortcut, people take the shortcut (P3b). So friction is measured and has a time-boxed escape.
4. **Nothing standing.** No standing prod write, no long-lived credentials.
5. **Evidence by construction.** The path itself produces the records; nobody writes them afterwards.

### Roles

| Role | Who | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Author | The engineer, and the agent working for them | Never approves their own change. An agent never approves (GĐ-11). |
| Approver | A named human with GitHub write access, listed in CODEOWNERS | ≠ author, ≠ last pusher, ≠ the person who triggered an app-authored PR (📖 R3.2.3, R3.3.4). |
| On-call approver | Primary + backup, 24/7, named in the on-call schedule | Same rule as Approver. Page target: approval wait ≤ 15 min (S7). |
| Platform approver | Platform team member | Second approval for L3 changes (layer 3). |
| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1) | Owns the policy files and metrics. Is **not** the only approver. |

---

## Layer 1 — Identity and access

**Principle**

- Every action traces to one named human. An agent acts for a human; it is never an anonymous
  shared identity.
- Nobody holds standing write access to production. Production is written by the pipeline role,
  or, in the fallback, by an approved, time-boxed human grant.
- Production reads default to metadata. Reading stores that hold customer data is blocked by a
  guardrail the agent cannot edit.
- No long-lived credentials anywhere. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Why the human's access is the agent's access.** On a laptop, the agent uses the engineer's
  AWS SSO cache, and that cache reaches every role assigned to the engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2).
  A separate "agent" permission set does not separate them (📖 R2.9 #1). So the control is what
  the **engineer** holds.
- **AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1):
  - `ProdReadMetadata`: read config, metrics and redacted log groups in prod; session duration 1 h,
    the minimum (📖 R2.1.4).
  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad rights in non-prod accounts only.
  - **No standing prod-write permission set** is assigned to anyone.
  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: exists, but is assigned only by the JIT flow (layer 7). Tooling
    options: a partner product, the TEAM sample, or a small flow on `CreateAccountAssignment` /
    `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.1, R2.4.1b, R2.4.2).
- **Guardrails in the prod OU (SCPs)**, which member-account principals cannot edit (📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
  - deny data-plane reads on stores that hold claim data (for example `s3:GetObject` on the claim
    documents bucket, `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`), except application roles
    and the approved data-read role, selected by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern from R2.9 #4, ⚠️ untested);
  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` and `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` except the
    CloudFormation `deploymentRole` and the named JIT roles. This closes `serverless deploy
    function` (📖 R4.4.4, R4.6 #3; SCP vs IAM not yet chosen, ⚠️);
  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:userId` (📖 R2.4.4);
  - protect the organization trail and log archive (📖 R2.6.2).
  Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters each, nothing applies to the management account
  (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4).
- **Sessions:** set the access-portal session length on purpose; the IdP session can silently
  extend it (📖 R2.1.5, R2.1.6). MFA lives in the external IdP if one is used (📖 R2.1.7).
- **CI → AWS:** GitHub OIDC, no stored keys (📖 R3.4.1). The prod deploy role trusts only
  `repo:<owner>@<owner-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>:environment:production` (immutable `sub` format, 📖 R3.4.4),
  customised to include `job_workflow_ref` of the reusable deploy workflow (📖 R3.4.5).
  Non-prod roles trust non-prod environments or `pull_request` (📖 R4.6 #2).
- **CI → GCP:** Workload Identity Federation with an attribute condition on Papaya's GitHub
  organization, which Google requires (📖 R3.4.5b). GCP can test `job_workflow_ref` directly
  (⚠️ inference in R3.4.5b).
- **Humans → GCP, k0s, Firebase:** the same principles apply (no standing prod write, metadata-only
  reads, federation). The mechanisms are **not researched** (⚠️ gap G1–G3 below). Interim rule: no
  admin kubeconfig and no GCP owner role on laptops; prod deploys to k0s and Firebase run only from CI.

**Audit evidence**

- Export of Identity Center assignments showing no standing prod-write assignment (S1).
- CloudTrail `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` for each JIT grant (📖 R2.4.2),
  linked to its approval record by request ID [design].
- SCP and trust-policy text in Pulumi code: version history = change history.
- IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` result on every PR that changes a policy (📖 R2.8.1).
- Quarterly access-review record (who holds which permission set).

**Cost / value.** Engineers lose standing prod write; in exchange they keep fast prod reads and a
free non-prod loop. Compliance gets least privilege that is enforced, not promised.

---

## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls

**Principle**

- Agent-side controls are a hygiene layer: they cut mistakes, they are not the boundary. The docs
  call managed settings "a client-side control, not a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7).
- They are set centrally, the same for everyone, and versioned in git.
- Safe defaults, with a measured escape hatch: a default that people constantly override is
  replaced, not defended.
- The session that reads untrusted content should not be the session that holds power (📖 R6.1.2).

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Delivery:** server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console (available on Team,
  📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. Where MDM exists, also an endpoint `managed-settings.json`, which a
  normal user cannot edit (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.8). MDM is unknown, so both paths are prepared (R1.9).
- **Baseline keys** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4):

  | Key | Value | Why | Source |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `permissions.defaultMode` | `default` (Manual) | Owner decision D1. A default, not a lock: users can switch to auto, and VS Code remembers the last pick. | 📖 R6.9.3 |
  | `permissions.allow` (managed) | read-only commands Papaya uses (e.g. `Bash(aws cloudwatch get-metric-data *)`) | Fewer prompts for safe reads (P3b) | 📖 R6.9.3 |
  | `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` | `true` | One rule set for everyone (D1, Q4) | 📖 R1.2.5 |
  | `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` | `"disable"` | Removes "prompts off" (P3a) | 📖 R1.2.2 |
  | `requiredMinimumVersion` | ≥ latest fixed advisory at rollout (≥ 2.1.260 at minimum) | Advisory history makes the version a control | 📖 R1.1.13, R6.3.10, R6.5 #4 |
  | `allowedProviders` + `forceLoginOrgUUID` | `["anthropic"]` + Papaya's org | Closes most bypasses on endpoint-managed machines | 📖 R1.1.15 |
  | `allowManagedHooksOnly` | `true` | Repo and user hooks cannot run | 📖 R1.5.4 |
  | `sandbox.enabled`, `sandbox.failIfUnavailable`, `sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, `sandbox.credentials` / `filesystem.denyRead` on `~/.aws`, narrow `network.allowedDomains` | on | The sandbox reads `~/.aws` by default (R1.6.3). Shell commands only (R1.6.2). | 📖 R1.6.4 |
  | MCP and plugin keys | see layer 4 | | |
  | OTel exporter, content flags `0` | on | Usage evidence without prompt content | 📖 R1.1.20, R5.5.4 |

- **Session types.** Each type has its own identity and flags:

  | Session | Where | Identity | Flags | Notes |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Daily development | laptop | non-prod roles + `ProdReadMetadata` | managed baseline | Auto mode allowed by choice (D1). |
  | Incident analysis | laptop | `ProdReadMetadata` only | `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"` | Process rule (D3, owner Q1–Q2): reads logs, proposes a fix, cannot edit. 📖 R6.9.1b |
  | CI agent (PR review, code tasks) | GitHub-hosted runner | its own GitHub App token; **no** prod environment | `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`, `--setting-sources user`, hooks disabled | 📖 R1.7.3, R3.6 #4, D3 |
  | JIT terminal (fallback only) | laptop | JIT grant | **no agent running** | Process rule (D2). |
  | Auto-mode sandbox (day 60–90) | separate environment, non-prod credentials only | non-prod | auto mode encouraged | D1 option (c). |

- **Hard limits to state openly:**
  - Bash permission rules are not a security boundary (📖 R1.2.6).
  - Hooks fail open unless `"onFailure": "block"` is set (📖 R1.5.2).
  - `--restricted` cannot be forced by a setting on laptops (📖 R6.9.1, R6.9.1c).
  - Server-managed settings are bypassed by a different login, an API key or a provider variable
    (📖 R1.1.7). On a laptop without MDM, `allowedProviders` from the server is the main counter.
  - In the JIT window, the grant sits in the same SSO cache the agent can reach (📖 R2.2.2). "No
    agent in the JIT terminal" is a process control (D2).
- **Fallback:** switch to `disableAutoMode` if the planted-injection test (layer 8) steers auto
  mode, a serious advisory appears, or an audit finds auto mode touched a protected scope (D1).

**Audit evidence**

- The managed settings file in git, with PR approvals (change history of the policy).
- `/status` and `claude doctor` output from a sample of machines (📖 R1.1.18).
- OTel: `claude_code.tool_decision` with `permission_mode`; `claude_code.tool.blocked_on_user`
  with `duration_ms` as a rubber-stamping signal (D1 metrics, 6.6).
- Settings-change audit events exist, but availability on Team is unknown (⚠️ R1.1.12).

**Cost / value.** Manual mode prompts more than auto mode; the managed read-only allowlist offsets
part of it. Compliance gets an organization policy with evidence, instead of personal choices (P3c).

---

## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level

**Principle**

- The level is set by the damage a change can do, not by who asks.
- Above non-prod, one path: a reviewed PR, applied by the pipeline. The approver reviews what will
  be applied, and is a named human who is not the author.
- Higher risk adds a second, specialised approver, not a different path.
- An incident uses the same path with faster people, not fewer checks.

**Levels**

| Level | What | Examples | Approval | Path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L0** | Read: anything in non-prod; metadata in prod | `aws lambda get-function-configuration`, CloudWatch metrics, redacted logs, `pulumi preview` on non-prod | None | Direct, read-only identity |
| **L1** | Change in non-prod (synthetic data only, GĐ-14) | Deploy a branch to dev, try a new queue setting | None beyond the author | Direct with non-prod roles, or a PR preview pipeline |
| **L2** | Routine prod change, expressible as code | Lambda timeout/memory, ECS desired count, app release | 1 approval: code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher | PR → merge to `main` → deploy workflow |
| **L3** | High-risk prod change | IAM or SCP; replace/delete of a stateful resource; network; `.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `.claude/**`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.mcp.json`, plugin catalogue; a policy-pack violation; a real-data read (layer 6); the JIT fallback (layer 7) | L2 + platform approver | Same PR path; second approval by path rule or by the deploy job's risk stop |

**On Papaya's stack**

- **The gate is the merge to `main`.** On GitHub Team, environment required reviewers are not
  available for private repos (📖 R3.1.2; Team is the owner's assumption GĐ-5). A ruleset on `main`
  sets (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.5):
  - require a pull request, 1 approval, code-owner review;
  - dismiss stale approvals when the diff changes;
  - require approval from someone other than the last person to push;
  - required status checks with a pinned source app;
  - block force pushes; empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2).
  GitHub already stops authors from approving their own PR (📖 R3.3.1).
- **L3 by path:** path-based required reviewers, e.g. 1 approval from `platform` on `infra/iam/**`
  and `.github/**` (📖 R3.2.4).
- **L3 by preview [design]:** the deploy job on `main` runs the prod preview. If it shows
  replace/delete of a stateful resource, an IAM change or a policy violation, it stops. The engineer
  opens a second PR adding `deploy-approvals/<sha>.yaml` with the preview hash; platform approves;
  the job re-runs and continues only if the hash matches (Options §1; hash stability ⚠️ Options §8).
- **Making "merge approval = deploy approval" true** (📖 R3.6 #1):
  - the `production` environment allows only `main` (📖 R3.1.3);
  - only the CODEOWNERS-protected reusable deploy workflow references `production`;
  - deploy workflows take no ref or SHA input and use no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or
    `workflow_run` trigger (📖 R3.4.5c);
  - one concurrency group per stack, without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4).
- **Pulumi:**
  - PRs preview **non-prod stacks only**, because a prod preview runs PR code with state-write and
    secret access (📖 R4.6 #2, R4.3.3);
  - on `main`: `pulumi preview` on prod, then `pulumi up` with the policy pack, which stops on a
    mandatory violation (📖 R4.2.2);
  - prod runs use an allowlist of commands: no `--target`, `--replace`, `--skip-preview`, no
    `state`, `import`, `destroy` (📖 R4.6 #3).
- **Serverless Framework (v4):**
  - `serverless package`, then `serverless diff --json` (sf-core ≥ 4.37.0). It always exits 0, so
    CI parses the JSON (📖 R4.4.2);
  - `serverless deploy --package` deploys the built artifact (📖 R4.4.3);
  - `provider.iam.deploymentRole` set, least privilege; it cannot be removed later (📖 R4.4.5).
- **Incident lane:** PR label `incident`; on-call approver paged; security checks always run (S10);
  only slow, unrelated tests are skipped [design]. Path filters on required checks may leave them
  pending (⚠️ Options §8).

**Example: Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m.** (Options §6)

1. The engineer's incident-analysis session (`--restricted`, read-only identity) reads metrics and
   redacted logs, and proposes: `timeout` 30 → 90 s, `memorySize` 1024 → 2048, plus the queue's
   visibility timeout.
2. A second session, with no prod identity, edits `serverless.yml` and runs `serverless diff` on
   non-prod. It opens a PR labelled `incident` under the engineer's GitHub identity.
3. The on-call approver reviews the diff and approves; the engineer merges.
4. The deploy workflow packages, previews prod, sees no risky change, deploys with the OIDC role.
5. Estimated 11–46 min (⚠️ unmeasured, Options §6). The target is ≤ 30 min, so measuring this lane
   is the first rollout task (layer 8).

**Audit evidence**

- The PR: diff, approvers, check results, labels.
- The run: prod preview artifact and deploy log, exported because run retention is limited (⚠️
  duration unknown, Options §8).
- CloudTrail events of the deploy role.
- All linked by commit SHA and run ID, kept ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.7 #2).

**Cost / value.** One approval for routine prod changes, two for risky ones; no approval in
non-prod. Compliance gets four-eyes enforced by GitHub, and a record per change. The open gap: on
Team, the reviewer sees the non-prod preview, not the prod diff.

---

## Layer 4 — Supply chain for MCP servers and plugins

**Principle**

- An MCP server or plugin is software that runs with the engineer's access (📖 R1.6.2, R5.5.5).
  It is installed only from a reviewed catalogue, pinned to a version.
- The catalogue is the inventory (P4c).
- Review must be fast (S6: ≤ 5 working days), or people will work around it.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Plugins:**
  - Papaya's private marketplace is a git repo with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` (📖 R1.4.1);
    sources pinned to a `ref` or `sha` (📖 R1.4.1b, link only).
  - Managed: `strictKnownMarketplaces` = Papaya's marketplace only; `blockedMarketplaces`;
    `enabledPlugins: false` to pull one plugin (📖 R1.4.2). The allowlist is checked before download
    and at every session start (📖 R1.4.3).
  - Client ≥ 2.1.179, which fixes a plugin-pin bypass (📖 R6.2.7).
  - Plugin hooks run only if the plugin is force-enabled in managed `enabledPlugins` (📖 R1.5.4).
    User-installed mods are blocked with `allowManagedModsOnly` (📖 R1.5.6).
- **MCP servers:**
  - "Approved catalogue" pattern: `allowedMcpServers` + `allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true`
    (📖 R1.3.1, R1.3.4). Without the lock, users can widen the list (📖 R1.3.4).
  - Match by `serverUrl` or `serverCommand`, never `serverName` ("not a security control",
    📖 R1.3.3). The `serverCommand` argv pins an exact version, not `@latest` (⚠️ inference, R6.4.4).
  - `disableClaudeAiConnectors: true` (📖 R1.3.7).
  - With MDM, `managed-mcp.json` gives exclusive control; it cannot be delivered server-managed
    (📖 R1.3.2).
- **Review checklist (one page per entry)** [design]:
  - publisher and licence; local (`stdio`) or remote (📖 R6.4.3);
  - what it can read and where it sends data; an entry in the supplier register with BAA/DPA status
    (📖 R5.6);
  - authentication: no token passthrough (📖 R6.4.2);
  - write tools (Slack, Linear, GitHub) enabled only where needed (📖 R6.5 #6);
  - pinned version; reviewer's name; review date.
- **Known gaps:** server-managed settings cannot target groups (📖 R1.1.6, R1.4.4); changes to a
  server's tool descriptions after approval are not covered (⚠️ R6.6).

**Audit evidence**

- The catalogue file in git: each addition is a PR with an approver.
- The supplier register.
- OTel `claude_code.plugin_installed` / `plugin_loaded` (📖 R1.4.6) and MCP tool usage with
  `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` (📖 R1.3.8).

**Cost / value.** Engineers wait up to 5 days for a new tool, and request it with a short form.
Compliance gets an asset inventory and supplier records for every extension.

---

## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening

**Principle**

- CI is the only production writer, so it is the most valuable target.
- No long-lived credentials; least-privilege, short-lived tokens per job.
- Every third-party dependency of CI is pinned.
- Code written by an agent goes through the same checks as code written by a person (S10).

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Credentials:**
  - replace AWS keys and long-lived tokens in repository secrets with OIDC (📖 R3.4.1). Anyone with
    write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b);
  - `GITHUB_TOKEN` default "restricted"; each job declares `permissions:` (📖 R3.5.3);
  - "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" stays **off** (📖 R3.3.3);
  - Serverless License Key in SSM per account, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8).
- **Close side paths to prod:** do not use Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments or Serverless Dashboard
  providers for prod. If used, they get the same trust and audit as the GitHub path (📖 R4.4.9, R4.6 #6).
- **Pin CI dependencies:** workflow lockfile (`gh actions-lock`) or full SHA, enforced by the org
  policy "Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" (📖 R3.5.5).
- **Protect the files that control CI and agents:** CODEOWNERS on `.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`,
  `.claude/`, `.mcp.json`, `.husky/`, `.gitmodules` (📖 R3.2.8, R6.5 #5). CI validates the CODEOWNERS
  file, because invalid lines are skipped silently (📖 R3.2.7).
- **No privileged triggers with untrusted code:** no `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` job
  that checks out PR code (📖 R3.5.4).
- **Agents in CI:**
  - `claude-code-action` with a custom GitHub App limited to Contents, Issues and Pull requests
    (📖 R1.7.8);
  - authentication through Anthropic workload identity federation, not a personal OAuth token
    (📖 R1.7.6);
  - `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`, repo hooks disabled (D3, 📖 R1.7.3);
  - never `environment: production` (📖 R3.6 #4);
  - a managed-settings file written on a GitHub-hosted runner is advisory, because the job has
    `sudo` (📖 R3.5.1);
  - an app-authored PR needs 2 approvals, or a pinned check confirming a human approver who did not
    trigger the run (📖 R3.3.4, R3.7 A3).
- **Required security checks on every PR to `main` (S10):** secret scanning, dependency check, SAST.
  The products are **not researched** (⚠️ gap G4). Two checks are researched: IAM Access Analyzer
  `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and Pulumi policy packs (📖 R4.2.2).

**Audit evidence**

- Workflow files and the lockfile in git.
- Org audit log events: `org.update_actions_secret`, `repo.set_workflow_permission_can_approve_pr`,
  `repository_ruleset.update` (📖 R3.3.3, R3.5.6).
- Check results attached to each PR.
- Inventory of repository secrets: target zero cloud credentials (S2).

**Cost / value.** One-time migration of workflows to OIDC and pinned actions; slower updates of
actions. Compliance gets S2 (no long-lived CI credentials) and the same guardrails for agent and
human code.

---

## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence

**Principle**

- By default the coding agent never sees real customer data (PHI and other sensitive data). This
  is enforced by what its identity can read, not by instructions (owner decision, R1.9).
- Reading real data is an exception: requested, approved, scoped to one tenant, time-boxed, done by
  a human (GĐ-9).
- Everything the agent reads from outside is untrusted: logs, tickets, PR text, web pages, MCP
  results, uploaded documents.
- Untrusted reading and write power are kept apart.
- Non-prod holds synthetic data only (GĐ-14).

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Close the paths by identity.** `work/02-research.md` 1.11.4 lists 17 ways PHI can reach the
  agent (logs, SQL, S3, queues, tickets, uploaded documents, exec, replay…). The main control is that
  agent-usable identities have **no data-plane read** on PHI stores (R1.11.4, R2.9 #4):
  - SCP deny on claim buckets and queues (layer 1);
  - no Aurora credentials for engineers' agents; no `ecs:ExecuteCommand`, `kubectl exec` or
    `lambda:InvokeFunction` in prod for agent-usable roles [design];
  - logs redacted at source, raw payloads in a separate log group that `ProdReadMetadata` cannot read
    [design];
  - alerts carry IDs and links, not payloads [design].
- **The real-data exception (GĐ-9)** [design]:
  - a request names the tenant, the purpose, the store and the time window; the data owner and an
    approver ≠ requester approve it (L3);
  - a JIT data-read role, tenant-scoped through session tags (ABAC, 📖 R2.1.8), TTL 1 h;
  - the human reads in a terminal without an agent; the agent only gets a redacted summary.
  - Reason: the Team plan is not covered by Anthropic's BAA (⚠️ R1.11.3.4), and the owner keeps
    the agent outside PHI scope. Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if a real need
    appears (R1.9).
- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b).** Never open a raw partner document in an agent
  session. Reproduce bugs with synthetic documents; if a real one is needed, a de-identification
  step comes first [design]. The document is both PHI and an injection vector (R1.11.4 L6).
- **Injection controls** (each lowers frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact):
  - Manual mode by default (layer 2); the auto-mode classifier misses some actions (17 % of 52 real
    overeager actions, 📖 R6.3.5);
  - narrow sandbox egress; a broad domain such as `github.com` is a documented exfiltration path
    (📖 R6.3.7);
  - incident analysis in `--restricted` with no edit tools (layer 2), so a poisoned log line can at
    most produce a bad *proposal* that a human reviews in a PR;
  - shared knowledge in `CLAUDE.md` under CODEOWNERS; personal auto memory is reviewed by the
    engineer and is a residual risk with a named owner (D3, 📖 R6.3.11).
- **Tenant isolation:** one tenant per data-read grant (ABAC tags); a session that read tenant X's
  data writes nothing to shared places (PRs, tickets, chat) without review (⚠️ process; R6.5 #8).
  Tenants are assumed to be separated logically in shared accounts (GĐ-3, unconfirmed).
- **Non-prod:** no copies from prod to non-prod (GĐ-14, S11); periodic scan of non-prod stores
  (tool not researched, ⚠️ gap G4).
- **Local stores:** session transcripts and memory hold what the agent read (R1.11.4). Set
  `cleanupPeriodDays` (the HIPAA sample uses 30, 📖 R5.5.4).
- **Cross-border (Vietnam example):** using a model provider outside Vietnam on Vietnamese personal
  data is a transfer; agent data flows update Papaya's existing transfer impact assessment (📖
  R5.4.5; application ⚠️ R5.7 #4, needs Papaya legal).

**Audit evidence**

- SCP and IAM text (the written access rule for sensitive data, 📖 R5.4.3 Art. 4(2), R5.7 #5).
- Data-read requests: requester, approver, tenant, window; CloudTrail of the data-read role.
- Planted-injection test reports (layer 8).
- Non-prod scan results (S11).

**Cost / value.** Engineers debug with redacted data and synthetic documents; the rare real-data
read needs a request. Compliance gets "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM, and a
record for every exception (S9).

---

## Layer 7 — Observability, audit, incident response and break-glass

**Principle**

- One evidence chain per production change: who proposed, who approved, what was approved, what was
  applied, when. Tamper-evident, retained ≥ 6 years.
- Every prod alert goes to one routed channel with a named on-call, including on-call approvers.
- Unapproved change is detected: drift and reconciliation are compliance signals.
- Break-glass is time-boxed, approved before use, and reconciled after.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Audit stores:**
  - an organization CloudTrail to a log-archive account, integrity validation on, retention chosen
    on purpose (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4, R2.6.5). Data events only on PHI buckets, prod Lambda invoke and
    prod SQS, because of cost (📖 R2.6.3). CloudTrail Lake is closed to new customers (📖 R2.6.6);
  - the GitHub org audit log keeps 180 days, so it is exported (📖 R3.5.6, R3.6 #6);
  - alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`,
    `environment.delete`, `protected_branch.policy_override` (📖 R3.6 #1);
  - Aurora: SQL is not in CloudTrail; Database Activity Streams, with an alert on lost-record events,
    and the stream treated as PHI (📖 R2.7.1, R2.7.2; Serverless v2 support ⚠️);
  - Claude Code OTel without prompt content (layer 2).
- **Change record [design]:** one record per prod change, keyed by commit SHA or JIT request ID,
  linking the PR, approvals, run ID, preview artifact and CloudTrail events. Monthly reconciliation:
  every prod write event in CloudTrail must match an approved record (S3). The actor is
  `onBehalfOf.userId` where present, otherwise the session name plus a directory lookup (📖 R2.5.1,
  R2.5.3; ⚠️ on member-account events).
- **Drift detection:** scheduled `pulumi preview --refresh --expect-no-changes` or
  `pulumi refresh --preview-only` (📖 R4.3.1, R4.3.2); CloudFormation drift detection for Serverless
  stacks, which checks only explicitly set properties (📖 R4.4.6). Auto-remediation stays off, since it
  is an unreviewed `up` (📖 R4.3.2). Each finding maps to a CloudTrail actor and a ticket.
- **On-call (phase 1 minimum):** a named schedule with primary and backup approvers, 24/7, and one
  alert route for prod. The paging and alert tools are not researched (⚠️ gap G5).
- **Break-glass = the JIT fallback (D2'):**

  | Step | Rule |
  |---|---|
  | When | Only if the PR path cannot be used: the operation is not in IaC and has no runbook, or GitHub/Actions is down, or the pipeline is broken. The approver refuses JIT for anything expressible in IaC while the pipeline works, and records why. |
  | Request | Exact command list, service scope, reason, incident link. |
  | Approval | On-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant. |
  | Grant | `InfraOperator-<service>`, session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). Removing the assignment stops only new sessions (📖 R2.4.3); an immediate stop needs the revocation SCP (📖 R2.4.4). |
  | Execution | The human types the commands in a terminal with no agent. The agent may propose them from its read-only session (D2). |
  | After | A reconciliation job compares CloudTrail writes in the window with the list [design]. A codify PR within a fixed deadline; drift detection until it merges. |
  | Identity Center outage | Emergency direct SAML federation to roles, built and tested in advance, with its own approval and alerting (📖 R2.1.11, R2.9 #2). |

  Metrics with review thresholds: JIT grants per month; JIT used for changes that should have gone
  through a PR; windows with writes outside the list; codify PRs past deadline (Options §7). When a
  threshold is passed, the fix is to make the PR lane faster or move the operation to a runbook,
  not to widen JIT.
- **Later (roadmap):** pre-approved runbooks for repeated non-IaC operations, if SSM Automation's
  approval step meets three conditions (Options §2, §7; this source is outside `02-research.md`,
  see G6); break-glass from an environment without the agent installed (D2, ⚠️).

**Audit evidence**

- CloudTrail with digest validation; exported GitHub audit log.
- Change records and the monthly reconciliation report (S3, S8: evidence for a random change in
  ≤ 30 min).
- JIT request records, reconciliation results, codify PRs.
- Drift reports and their tickets.
- On-call schedule and approval-wait times (S7).

**Cost / value.** The incident lane is slower than direct access (estimated 11–46 min vs 2–20,
Options §6), and engineers must write a command list for JIT. Compliance gets approval before apply
even in incidents, and detection when something slips through.

---

## Layer 8 — Governance and rollout

**Principle**

- Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date.
- Policies live in git and change through PRs, like code.
- Access is never removed before its replacement works (otherwise people break the rule in the
  first incident).
- Controls are tested against real attacks, not only reviewed on paper.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Ownership:**

  | Area | Owner |
  |---|---|
  | Framework, managed settings, MCP/plugin catalogue, metrics | DevSecOps |
  | Deploy workflows, rulesets, Pulumi/Serverless pipelines | Platform team |
  | Evidence review, supplier register, ISO Statement of Applicability | Compliance |
  | CODEOWNERS for each domain | Engineering leads |
  | On-call schedule (incl. approvers) | Engineering management |

- **Policy as code:** managed settings, the MCP/plugin catalogue, SCPs, trust policies, CODEOWNERS
  and deploy workflows are files in the monorepo under CODEOWNERS. GitHub settings that are not files
  (rulesets, environment config) are compared with an expected copy by a scheduled job (📖 R3.6 #1;
  endpoint ⚠️).
- **Metrics** (from framing §5): S1 standing prod-write = 0; S2 cloud credentials in GitHub
  secrets = 0; S3 unmatched prod changes = 0; S4 approval wait ≤ 1 h; S5 machines with the policy =
  100 %; S6 tools outside the catalogue = 0; S7 incident approval wait ≤ 15 min; S8 evidence in
  ≤ 30 min; S9 data reads without approval = 0; S10 PRs with checks = 100 %; S11 prod copies in
  non-prod = 0.
- **Rollout** (≈ 90 days, GĐ-12 unconfirmed). Order from framing round 1 Q8, with the on-call
  approver list moved into phase 1:

  | Phase | Days | Items |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | 0–30 | OIDC for all deploy workflows, remove AWS keys and long-lived tokens; rulesets and CODEOWNERS on `main`; on-call approver schedule (primary + backup); managed settings baseline; MCP/plugin catalogue v1; **measure the incident PR lane on one real service** (target ≤ 30 min). |
  | 2 | 30–60 | Remove standing prod write (only after the approver schedule and JIT fallback work); SCP data-plane deny; drift detection; audit-log export and change records; Aurora activity streams. |
  | 3 | 60–90 | Planted-injection test on the real configuration (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.5, R6.5 #12); auto-mode non-prod environment (D1 c); verify the SSM runbook option; first evidence pack for ISO 27001; 90-day review of D1–D3. |

- **Exceptions:** any deviation from this framework is a ticket with an owner, a reason and an
  expiry date.
- **Mapping to standards:** HIPAA Security Rule sections are cited from the text (📖 R5.2); ISO/IEC
  27001:2022 Annex A control IDs are recalled, not read, and must be checked against a licensed copy
  (⚠️ R5.1). The "named human approves" rule is Papaya's chosen way to meet change-management and
  segregation-of-duties controls, not a literal requirement (⚠️ R5.7 #1).
- **Out of scope:** security of Papaya's production AI agents (A7a). Noted as a follow-up.

**Audit evidence**

- Git history of every policy file.
- Monthly metric report; 90-day review minutes; exception register.
- Planted-injection test reports.

**Cost / value.** A small, steady overhead for DevSecOps and platform. Compliance gets a managed
system with owners and review dates, which ISO 27001 auditors look for.

---

## Gaps: things this framework needs but `work/02-research.md` does not cover

These are named at the level of principle only. Each needs research before `examples/` uses it.

| # | Gap | Where it matters |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | k0s: authentication (OIDC?), RBAC, audit logging, how kubeconfigs are issued | Layers 1, 6 |
| G2 | Firebase Hosting deploy from CI without a long-lived token | Layers 1, 5 |
| G3 | Engineer and agent access to GCP (roles, read-only, data access) | Layers 1, 6 |
| G4 | Secret scanning, dependency check, SAST, non-prod data scanning: which tools, on the Team plan | Layers 5, 6 |
| G5 | Paging and alert routing (on-call tool); approval from a phone | Layer 7 |
| G6 | SSM Automation `aws:approve` (read in `work/03-options.md` §2 on 2026-11-09, not in 02-research) | Layer 7 roadmap |
| G7 | Retention of GitHub Actions logs and artifacts; how to export them | Layers 3, 7 |
| G8 | Rulesets and environment settings as code (API/Terraform-like management) | Layer 8 |
| G9 | How Linear and Slack MCP servers authenticate (whose identity posts) | Layers 4, 6 |

Open checks carried over from `work/03-options.md` §8 (preview hash stability, required checks
skipped by path filters, Identity Center provisioning time, and others) remain open.
