## Layer 4 — Supply chain for MCP servers and plugins

**Principle.** Local MCP servers, plugins and hooks run with the engineer's access (📖 R1.6.2, R5.5.5); remote MCP servers receive tokens and data.
Only reviewed, pinned entries from a catalogue are allowed. The catalogue is the inventory (P4c).
Review takes ≤ 5 working days (S6), or people work around it.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Plugins:** a private marketplace repo with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` (📖 R1.4.1), sources
  pinned to `ref`/`sha` (📖 R1.4.1b, link only). Managed `strictKnownMarketplaces` = Papaya only,
  `blockedMarketplaces`, `enabledPlugins: false` to pull one (📖 R1.4.2), checked before download and
  at session start (📖 R1.4.3). `disableSideloadFlags` rejects `--plugin-dir`, `--plugin-url`,
  `--agents`, `--mcp-config` but not `.mcp.json` or `claude mcp add` (📖 R1.4.2). With
  `allowManagedHooksOnly`, plugin hooks run only for force-enabled plugins (📖 R1.5.4). User mods are
  blocked by the `allowManagedModsOnly` option under `pluginConfigs` → `cc-plugin-sec-default@builtin`
  → `options` (📖 R1.5.6). The version floor covers the plugin-pin fix of 2.1.179 (📖 R6.2.7).
- **MCP:** "approved catalogue" = `allowedMcpServers` + `allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true`; without
  the lock users can widen it (📖 R1.3.1, R1.3.4). Match by `serverUrl` or `serverCommand`, never
  `serverName` ("not a security control", 📖 R1.3.3); `serverCommand` matches the exact argv (📖 R1.3.3), so the catalogue entry pins an exact package version in it [design].
  `disableClaudeAiConnectors: true` (📖 R1.3.7). With MDM, `managed-mcp.json` gives exclusive control;
  it cannot come from server-managed settings (📖 R1.3.2).
- **Review checklist** [design]: publisher; local `stdio` or remote (📖 R6.4.3); what it reads and where
  it sends data, with a supplier-register entry and BAA/DPA status (⚠️ R5.6); no token passthrough
  (📖 R6.4.2); write tools for Slack, Linear, GitHub only where needed (⚠️ R6.5 #6); how the server authenticates (Linear and Slack: G9); pinned version,
  reviewer, date.
- **Known gaps:** no per-group targeting in server-managed settings (📖 R1.1.6, R1.4.4); tool
  description changes after approval are not covered (⚠️ research 6.6).

**Audit evidence.** Catalogue file in git (each entry = an approved PR); supplier register; OTel
`claude_code.plugin_installed` / `plugin_loaded` (📖 R1.4.6). MCP tool logging needs
`OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` (📖 R1.3.8); it stays off until we know whether it logs tool inputs (⚠️).

**Cost / value.** Up to 5 days' wait for a new tool. Compliance gets an asset inventory and supplier
records.

---

## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening

**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
checks as human code (S10).

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). Org default for `GITHUB_TOKEN` set to "restricted", `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
  deploys may need a stored credential in GitHub: a kubeconfig or token for k0s, a Firebase token or
  service-account key for Firebase Hosting. The owner accepts this as an exception to S2 = 0 until it
  is checked whether k0s and Firebase deploys can use OIDC (OD1, OD6). Conditions [design]:
  - stored only as an **environment secret of `production`**, never as a repository secret. Anyone
    with write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b), which would turn the exception into
    standing prod write for every engineer and their agent. Environment secrets and a deployment
    branch rule limited to `main` are available on Team for private repos (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3), and
    only the reviewed deploy workflow references the environment (layer 3);
  - the deploy job runs on GitHub-hosted runners. On self-hosted runners, jobs "are not run in an
    isolated container, even if they use environments", so environment secrets there must be
    treated like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5). Self-hosted runners "can be persistently
    compromised by untrusted code" from anyone who can open a PR, and runner groups limit only which
    repositories use them (📖 R3.5.2); in a monorepo any workflow can likely target the runner's label (⚠️ G15).
    How to restrict a runner to one workflow is not researched (⚠️ G15); just-in-time runners exist
    (📖 R3.5.2, not read in detail). If reaching k0s needs a self-hosted runner, that
    runner is dedicated to the `production` deploy, and the residual risk is recorded;
  - that environment secret is the single source of truth: no copy elsewhere (OD1);
  - an owner, an expiry and rotation in the exception register;
  - optionally a separate environment (e.g. `production-k0s`), limited to `main` and referenced
    only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy jobs cannot read these secrets
    [design].

  Residual risk: admins can change the environment, and a deleted environment comes back without
  protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); the alerts and settings comparison in layer 7 cover this. The exception
  covers **CI deploy credentials only**. Runtime credentials, such as a k0s autoscaler's AWS access to
  add or remove nodes, live in the cluster, not in GitHub; they follow layer 1 (no static keys, a
  role attached to the machine; ⚠️ not researched for k0s, G1).
- **Side paths:** Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard providers reach AWS
  (📖 R4.4.9) outside the GitHub gate (⚠️ R4.4.9); not used for prod (⚠️ R4.6 #6).
- **Pinning:** workflow lockfile (`gh actions-lock`) or full SHA, enforced by the org policy "Require
  actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" (availability on Team ⚠️); the lockfile does not pin reusable workflows, so
  the deploy workflow lives in the same repo (📖 R3.5.5; conclusion [design]).
- **CODEOWNERS** on `.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`,
  `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, `.devcontainer/` (📖 R3.2.8; list ⚠️ R6.5 #5, R6.3.11), plus
  `.npmrc` (registry redirection) [design], the policy packs, the SCP code and the
  catalogue file. This is the canonical L3 path list that layer 3 refers to. Not on it:
  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/`, owned by the stack's owners and the on-call group (OD8, OD9). The private plugin
  marketplace is a separate repo and needs its own ruleset and CODEOWNERS [design]. CI validates the file, because
  invalid lines are skipped silently (📖 R3.2.7).
- **No privileged triggers with untrusted code** (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` + checkout,
  📖 R3.5.4).
- **Agent review:** an independent agent (not the one that made the change) may post an automated
  review as an extra check; it never counts as an approval (GĐ-11).
- **Agents in CI:** `claude-code-action` with a custom GitHub App limited to Contents, Issues, Pull
  requests (📖 R1.7.8), whose own credentials are listed in the S2 inventory (⚠️ G19); Anthropic workload identity federation, not a personal OAuth token (📖 R1.7.6);
  `--restricted` and explicit `--tools` (D3; passing it through `claude_args` unverified, ⚠️ research
  6.9.4 Q5); a managed-settings file on the runner, which also guards against mods (📖 R1.5.6; for
  federation auth ⚠️); MCP set fixed by CI because `.mcp.json` loads without a prompt in `-p` runs
  (📖 R1.3.5); never `environment: production` (⚠️ R3.6 #4). Hosted runners give `sudo` (📖 R3.5.1),
  so with `Bash` in `--tools` the runner file is advisory (⚠️ R3.5.1, R3.6 #4).
- **App-opened PRs:** a required check set by a dedicated GitHub App, pinned as its source (layer 3), confirms at least one approval by a
  human who did not trigger the run; counting approvals is not enough, since the app's own approval
  might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3; 📖 R3.2.5).
- **Required checks (S10):** from phase 1, secret scanning, dependency check, SAST (products: G4);
  from phase 2, IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and Pulumi policy packs
  (📖 R4.2.2). For Serverless stacks, Access Analyzer would check the IAM policies in the
  CloudFormation template that `serverless package` produces, against the deployed ones (⚠️ not
  researched); policy packs do not apply to them. Until phase 2, the only compensation for OD8 is
  the risk stop, which fires on every IAM change in the prod preview.

**Audit evidence.** Workflows and lockfile in git; audit-log events such as
`org.update_actions_secret`, `repo.set_workflow_permission_can_approve_pr`, `repository_ruleset.update`
(📖 R3.3.3, R3.5.6). An audit event for environment-secret changes was not researched (⚠️); the
settings comparison in layer 7 covers the S2 exception meanwhile. Check results per PR; secrets inventory (S2).

**Cost / value.** One-time migration to OIDC and pinned actions; slower action updates. Compliance
gets S2 and the same guardrails for agent and human code.

---

## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence

**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role from
    phase 1 (existing broad read roles are removed) and the SCP from phase 2
    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. At night the data owner is not on call: the
  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day. This
  applies to non-PHI and PHI alike; for PHI the reader is still a human without an agent. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent (process rule, layer 1); the agent gets a
    redacted summary. This
    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9). Claim
    tables mix health, ID and bank data (research 1.11.4 L2), so a store that holds PHI is treated as
    PHI unless the agent reads a view or extract without PHI [design].
- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
  1.11.4 L6).
- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default (sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, layer 2); the auto-mode
  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions and 5.7 % of 1,000 synthetic exfiltration
  attempts (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path
  (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no WebFetch, likely no edit tools (layer 2), and runs outside
  the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
  commands (layer 2), including the SSO token cache; "no standing write, no PHI read" limits what
  the token opens, except during a JIT or data-read window (layer 2 mitigations). Shared knowledge
  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is exempt from the protected-path rules unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed
  (GĐ-3, unconfirmed).
- **Non-prod:** no prod copies (S11). A scan of non-prod stores runs at the start of phase 1 (tool:
  G4); a store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule (GĐ-14: until cleaned, non-prod follows the GĐ-9 data-read rule). Cost: until scanned, that store is
  not part of the free loop.
- **Local stores:** transcripts and memory hold what the agent read (research 1.11.4); set
  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).
- **Cross-border (Vietnam example):** processing data collected in Vietnam on a platform abroad is a
  transfer (📖 R5.4.5); agent flows, including employee names in logs and transcripts, update the
  transfer impact assessment (⚠️ R5.7 #4, needs Papaya legal).

**Audit evidence.** SCP/IAM text as the written access rule for sensitive data (📖 R5.4.3; ⚠️ R5.7 #5);
data-read requests and the data-read role's CloudTrail; planted-injection reports (layer 8); non-prod
scan results (S11).

**Cost / value.** Debugging with redacted and synthetic data; a request for the rare real-data read.
Compliance gets "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM for AWS stores (fully from phase 2;
actions ⚠️ G13) and by process
elsewhere, and a record per exception (S9).

---

## Layer 7 — Observability, audit, incident response and break-glass

**Principle.** One tamper-evident evidence chain per prod change. One routed alert channel with a
named on-call, approvers included. Unapproved change is detected (drift, reconciliation). Break-glass
is approved before use, time-boxed and reconciled after.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Audit stores:**
  - organization CloudTrail to a log-archive account with integrity validation (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4,
    R2.6.5); change records ≥ 6 years; raw-log retention for Papaya's compliance owner (⚠️ R5.7 #2).
    Data events only on PHI buckets, prod Lambda invoke and prod SQS (cost 📖 R2.6.3; selection
    ⚠️ R2.9 #5), which makes the archive
    PHI-bearing (⚠️ research 1.11.4 L15). CloudTrail Lake is closed to new customers (📖 R2.6.6);
  - GitHub org audit log kept 180 days, so exported (📖 R3.5.6);
  - alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`,
    `environment.remove_protection_rule`, `environment.delete`, `protected_branch.policy_override`
    (📖 R3.5.6, R3.1.4; selection ⚠️ R3.6 #1). UI changes to the branch policy may leave no event, and a
    deleted `production` environment comes back unprotected (⚠️ R3.1.4): a job compares live settings
    with an expected copy (G8);
  - Aurora SQL is likely invisible to CloudTrail (⚠️ R2.7.1): Database Activity Streams, alerts on
    lost-record events (📖 R2.7.2; Serverless v2 ⚠️), stream treated as PHI (⚠️ R2.7.3);
  - Claude Code OTel without prompt content (layer 2).
- **Change record [design]:** keyed by commit SHA or JIT request ID; links PR, approvals, run ID,
  preview and CloudTrail events. Monthly reconciliation: every prod write event matches a record
  approved before apply (S3). Actor: `onBehalfOf.userId` where present, else session name plus
  directory lookup (📖 R2.5.1; ⚠️ R2.5.3).
- **Drift [design]:** its own role, trusted only from a `drift` environment on `main`; it can read
  prod secrets in state, which is noted (⚠️ R4.6 #2). Scheduled `pulumi preview --refresh
  --expect-no-changes` or `pulumi refresh --preview-only` (📖 R4.1.1, R4.3.1, R4.3.2). On a DIY S3
  backend, preview needs state-write permission (📖 R4.3.3); whether a refresh preview writes more
  than locks is open (⚠️ R4.6 #2, G14). So either the drift role gets state write (and the same
  trust care as the deploy role), or Pulumi Cloud drift detection is used (📖 R4.3.2, Pro+). The
  latter runs on Pulumi Deployments, which holds credentials to prod, so it re-opens a side path that
  layer 5 excludes and needs the same trust narrowing and audit (📖 R4.4.9; ⚠️ R4.6 #6). CloudFormation
  drift detection, explicitly set properties only (📖 R4.4.6). No auto-remediation: it is an unreviewed
  `pulumi up --refresh` (📖 R4.3.2). Each finding gets an actor and a ticket.
- **On-call:** phase 1 delivers the named approver schedule (primary + backup engineers, 24/7), as
  decided in framing round 1, and, because of OD7, a minimal incident-responder schedule; the
  latter extends that decision. The primary approves; the backup steps in only if the primary is
  unavailable (OD2). On-call approvers only approve during their shift; the fix is written by an
  incident responder (OD7). Alert routing and the
  rest of on-call follow in phase 2 (tools: G5); in phase 1 the responder calls the approver by phone from the published schedule.
- **Break-glass = JIT fallback** [design unless marked]:

  | Step | Rule |
  |---|---|
  | When | Only during an incident (Options §9 Q2), when the PR path cannot be used: operation not in IaC and no runbook; GitHub/Actions down; pipeline broken. The approver refuses JIT for anything expressible in IaC while the pipeline works, and records why. Outside incidents, an operation not in IaC waits for IaC or a runbook. |
  | Request | Command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub. |
  | Approval | On-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant (Options §4b; OD7; backup rule OD2). |
  | Grant | `InfraOperator-<service>`; role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). Deleting the assignment likely stops only new sessions (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3), so the real window can approach 2 h; ending the portal session does not end role sessions (📖 R2.4.3). An immediate stop needs the revocation SCP, which must keep the user blocked for at least 12 h (📖 R2.4.4). Applying it is a management-account change held by the L3 owner team only, and no night-time path for it is designed yet (⚠️ G20): until one exists, a misused grant may run to the end of its window. Candidate: a pre-approved revocation runbook for one named L3 owner reachable by phone, or an org-wide `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as kill switch (⚠️ R2.9 #3). |
  | Execution | The grant goes to the requester (the incident responder), who types the commands; no agent in that terminal (D2). D2 said the on-call person runs them; OD7 moves that to the responder, since on-call engineers only approve. |
  | After | A job compares CloudTrail writes in the window with the list; a codify PR within a fixed deadline (as soon as GitHub is back); drift detection until it merges. |
  | Identity Center outage | Emergency SAML federation to roles, built and tested in advance (📖 R2.1.11; ⚠️ R2.9 #2); no user mapped until an approved activation, which is alerted. |

  **Example request (illustrative command ⚠️):** "INC-123, ECS service `claims-api`, Actions outage. Run
  `aws ecs update-service --cluster <prod-cluster> --service <svc> --force-new-deployment`. Scope
  `InfraOperator-claims`, 1 h."

  **Metrics** (Options §7; starting thresholds ⚠️ to calibrate): JIT used where a PR was possible
  (review at 1); writes outside the list (review at 1); codify PRs late (review at 1); grants per
  month and share of incidents needing non-IaC operations (review above about 25 %, a value new in
  this draft). On a breach,
  make the PR lane faster or add a runbook; do not widen JIT.
- **Roadmap:** runbooks for repeated non-IaC operations, if SSM Automation's approval step meets three
  conditions (Options §2; outside 02-research, G6); break-glass from an environment without the agent
  (D2, ⚠️).

**Audit evidence.** Validated CloudTrail; exported GitHub audit log; change records and monthly
reconciliation (S3, S8 ≤ 30 min); JIT requests, reconciliations, codify PRs; drift tickets; on-call
schedule and approval waits (S7); monthly report of cross-domain approvals by on-call group members
on PRs without the `incident` label (OD9).

**Cost / value.** The incident lane is slower than direct access (estimated 11–46 vs 2–20 min,
Options §6), and JIT needs a written command list. Compliance gets approval before apply even in
incidents, plus detection.

---

## Layer 8 — Governance and rollout

**Principle.** Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date. Policies are files changed by
PR. Access is never removed before its replacement works. Controls are tested against realistic
attacks.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Owners:** DevSecOps (framework, managed settings, catalogue, metrics); a platform team or named
  engineers (deploy workflows, rulesets, pipelines; whether Papaya has a platform team is unknown ⚠️); Compliance (evidence review, supplier register, Statement of
  Applicability); engineering leads (decide CODEOWNERS content; changes to it are approved by the L3 owner team); engineering management (on-call schedule).
- **Policy as code:** catalogue, SCPs, trust policies, CODEOWNERS and workflows are files under
  CODEOWNERS. Settings that live outside files are kept as an expected copy in git and compared with
  the live state: GitHub settings (⚠️ R3.6 #1; G8) and Claude managed settings, which are edited in
  the admin console (📖 R1.1.5; comparison method in layer 2). Few GitHub admins and Claude org

# Architecture decision records

Each record states one major decision behind [`../framework.md`](../framework.md), the options weighed

# ADR-0001: Every production change goes through a reviewed PR applied by CI

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9, "A + D2'")
- **Scope:** all writes to production AWS, k0s and Firebase; incidents included

## 1. Context

Engineering wants Claude Code to talk to AWS directly; Compliance wants no production change without
a named human who reviewed and approved it. Today engineers can deploy from laptops (GĐ-10,
unconfirmed), so an agent on that laptop can deploy too. Incidents are where the pressure to bypass
review is highest.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. PR → approval → CI deploy for everything ("IaC first") | One path, approval before apply, evidence by construction | Slower incidents (est. 11–46 min ⚠️ vs 2–20 min, Options §6) |
| B. SSM Automation runbooks with an approval step | Approval inside AWS | Not verified that it meets the approval rule (G6); only for operations someone scripted |
| C. JIT direct access for the engineer + agent | Fastest | Approves access, not the change; agent holds prod write |
| D. Hosted agent with its own identity | Clean separation | New platform; does not remove the need for approval |

## 3. Decision

Option A is the default path for every production change, incidents included. A narrow JIT
fallback exists only when the PR path cannot be used during an incident (ADR-0005). The owner accepts
that this fallback meets the approval rule only partly (Options §9 Q2). Incident target: ≤ 30 min from
decision to apply.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** the PR, its approvals, the run log and CloudTrail form one evidence chain keyed by
  commit SHA. Agent-written and human-written changes pass the same checks (S10).
- **Negative / trade-offs:** slower incident fixes; operations that are not in IaC must first be
  written as code or a runbook. Two write paths remain (PR and JIT), while the framing asked for one.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** the fallback stays narrow only if most incidents are expressible in
  IaC (unknown, Options §8). Metrics: JIT grants per month, share of incidents needing non-IaC
  operations; above about 25 %, make the PR lane faster or add a runbook, never widen JIT.
- **Next steps:** measure the incident PR lane on one service first (phase 1).

## 6. References

- Framework §1 and layer 3; `work/03-options.md` §1, §6, §9.
- Related: ADR-0002, ADR-0003, ADR-0005.

# ADR-0002: Nobody holds standing prod write; the agent's identity is read-only metadata

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9; D2)
- **Scope:** AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets and SCPs on the prod OU; k0s and GCP by the same principle

## 1. Context

On a laptop the agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and one portal session reaches every role
assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate "agent"
permission set therefore does not separate the agent from the engineer (⚠️ R2.9 #1). Whatever the
engineer holds, the agent holds.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Separate agent permission set, engineer keeps write | Looks like least privilege | Same SSO cache: the agent can still assume the write role |
| B. No standing prod write for anyone; `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role | Agent cannot write prod with the engineer's identity | Engineers also lose direct writes and raw-log reads |
| C. Separate OS user or container for agent sessions | Real separation of credentials | More setup; planned for phase 3 only |

## 3. Decision

Option B. Prod is written only by the CI pipeline role, or by an approved, time-boxed JIT grant
(ADR-0005). The standing prod role is `ProdReadMetadata` [design name]: metrics, redacted log groups,
configuration of services whose secrets are resolved at runtime; no data-plane reads of claim stores;
1-hour role session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). SCPs on the prod OU deny data-plane reads and direct
Lambda updates except for named roles (pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4, R4.6 #3). Option C follows in phase 3.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** an agent, even a manipulated one, cannot write prod or read customer data with the
  engineer's standing identity. Compliance gets least privilege enforced by IAM (S1).
- **Negative / trade-offs:** during the transition, engineers lose raw logs and configuration of
  services not yet redacted; they need a data-read grant in an incident. Process rules remain where
  IAM cannot separate engineer and agent: no agent in the JIT terminal (D2).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** SSO-token theft during a session could open later grants (⚠️);
  mitigations are a short portal session and a fresh sign-in before a grant. The data-plane action
  list is incomplete (⚠️ G13). Identity Center assignment export is reviewed quarterly.
- **Next steps:** phase 1 removes broad read roles only after the minimal real-data read flow works,
  then removes standing prod write once its prerequisites are in place.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 1, layer 2 ("Trade-off on AWS credentials"), layer 8 rollout.
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0005, ADR-0009.

# ADR-0003: The merge to `main` is the approval gate: two people, code owners, on-call co-ownership

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-5, GĐ-8, GĐ-11; OD2, OD5, OD7, OD9, OD10, OD13)
- **Scope:** GitHub monorepo rulesets, CODEOWNERS, `production` environment, on-call schedule

## 1. Context

On GitHub Team, environment required reviewers do not exist for private repositories (📖 R3.1.2), so
the deploy job cannot wait for an approval. The approval must happen earlier. Incidents need an
approver within 15 minutes, 24/7 (S7), and code-owner review means the approver must own the files.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Upgrade to Enterprise for environment reviewers | Approval sits next to the deploy | Cost; not assumed (GĐ-5) |
| B. Merge to `main` as the gate; `production` limited to `main` | Works on Team; the approver sees the code that will be applied | Nobody sees the prod diff before apply (handled by ADR-0004) |
| C. More approvers for high-risk changes | More eyes | Slower; the owner wants two people per change |

## 3. Decision

Option B. Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, empty
bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). `production` accepts only `main` (📖 R3.1.3).

- **Two people per change:** one makes it, one approves it; the approver is always an engineer,
  never an agent (OD2, OD5). L3 changes need one approver too, who must own the path.
- **Incidents:** on-call engineers only approve; an incident responder writes the fix (OD7).
- **Night coverage:** an on-call approver group co-owns every deployable path in CODEOWNERS; one
  primary, one backup (OD9). It does not co-own process-defining paths (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS,
  agent config, catalogue) or the SCP stack, which only the L3 owner team approves (OD13).
- **Cross-team PRs:** one approval is enough (OD10).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** four-eyes enforced by GitHub, not by the agent. One rule for normal days and incidents.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** GitHub accepts an approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so the
  on-call group can approve another domain's PR; domain review on normal days is a process rule.
  One reviewer for high-risk changes can miss things (owner's trade-off for speed).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can edit the gate (logged, not prevented, 📖 R3.2.2);
  alerts on ruleset changes and a monthly report of cross-domain approvals on PRs without the
  `incident` label. An agent could approve through its engineer's login; no detection found (⚠️).
- **Next steps:** rulesets, CODEOWNERS and its validation check in phase 1; the composition of the L3
  owner team is open (G17).

## 6. References

- Framework layer 3 ("Gate = merge to `main`", "Who approves at night"), layer 7 (audit alerts).
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004.

# ADR-0004: Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until a stack owner approves the prod preview

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (OD8, OD11, OD13)
- **Scope:** deploy workflows for Pulumi and Serverless stacks; k0s and Firebase not covered yet

## 1. Context

With the gate at merge time (ADR-0003), the approver reviews the code change, not the prod diff. A
PR may not preview prod, because that would run PR code with state-write and secret access
(📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). So a stateful delete or an IAM change can reach prod without anyone
seeing its real effect. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files such as
`serverless.yml`, not in separate L3 paths.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Accept the gap | No extra step | Destructive diffs applied unseen |
| B. Risk stop, approved by the L3 owner team | Specialist review | Often a third person; L3 team must be on call 24/7 |
| C. Risk stop, approved by an owner of the stack | Stays at two people; works at night | Less specialist review; compensated by automated checks |

## 3. Decision

Option C [design]. The deploy job on `main` previews prod. On stateful replace/delete, an IAM
change, a network or security-group change, or (from phase 2) an advisory policy finding, it stops
and posts the filtered preview. The original author opens a PR adding
`deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml` with the SHA and preview hash; the first approver approves it
(OD13). If that approver is unavailable, another stack owner approves; this makes three people and
is recorded as a deviation (OD11). After the merge the workflow previews again on the new HEAD and
continues only if the hash matches. Serverless uses `serverless diff --json`, parsed by CI because
differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2). A `mandatory` Pulumi policy violation always
blocks `pulumi up` (📖 R4.2.2).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** the person who approves now sees the prod diff for the changes that can do lasting
  damage. Still two people in the normal case.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** a stopped stack blocks later merges to it, including an incident fix,
  until the approval lands or the change is reverted. One more review round when the stop fires.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** preview output may not be stable enough to hash (⚠️ Options §8); if
  not, compare a structured summary. Until phase 2, the risk stop is the only compensation for OD8;
  Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and policy packs follow. k0s and Firebase have no
  preview step in this design (⚠️ G1, G2).
- **Next steps:** risk stop in the deploy job in phase 1.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 3 ("Risk stop"), layer 5 (required checks); `work/03-options.md` §1.
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0003.

# ADR-0005: Break-glass is a time-limited, approved JIT grant, for incidents only

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9 Q2; D2; OD7, OD13)
- **Scope:** AWS production accounts through IAM Identity Center; k0s and Firebase not covered (G1, G2)

## 1. Context

Some incidents cannot use the PR path: GitHub or Actions is down, the pipeline is broken, or the
operation is not in IaC and has no runbook. Without a defined fallback, people keep standing access
"just in case", which ADR-0002 removes.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. No fallback | Single path | Outage of GitHub blocks every fix; pressure to keep standing access |
| B. Standing break-glass account | Always available | Standing prod write; hard to audit |
| C. Approved JIT grant, 1-hour role session, command list, reconciled after | Approval before use; time-boxed; traceable | Approves a command list, not an applied change (partial) |

## 3. Decision

Option C, used only during an incident when the PR path cannot be used.

- **Request:** command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub.
- **Approval:** the on-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant; the on-call approver counts as
  owner of the service (OD13).

  via `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2); role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4).

  fixed deadline; drift detection runs until it merges.

  a reconciliation.

  can run up to about 2 h (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3). An immediate stop needs the revocation SCP, which keeps

  automated reconciliation in phase 2.

- Framework layer 7 ("Break-glass = JIT fallback"); `work/03-options.md` §4b, §9.
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0002.

# ADR-0006: MCP servers and plugins are allowed only from a reviewed, pinned catalogue

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (framing Q8; OD4)
- **Scope:** Claude Code on all engineer laptops and in CI; Papaya's internal plugin marketplace

## 1. Context

Local MCP servers, plugins and hooks run with the engineer's access (📖 R1.6.2, R5.5.5); remote MCP
servers receive tokens and data. Papaya already runs an internal plugin marketplace and uses MCP for
Linear and Slack. An unreviewed server or a plugin update can read the repo, the SSO cache or claim
data and send it out.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Free choice, guidance only | No friction | No inventory; any server can exfiltrate |
| B. Denylist known-bad servers | Low friction | Misses new and changed servers |
| C. Allowlist (catalogue) enforced by managed settings | Inventory and supplier records; blocks unknown servers | Up to 5 working days' wait for a new tool (S6) |

## 3. Decision

Option C. The catalogue is a file in git, changed by PR under the L3 owner team.

- **Plugins:** only Papaya's marketplace via managed `strictKnownMarketplaces`, plus
  `blockedMarketplaces` (📖 R1.4.2); sources pinned to `ref`/`sha` (📖 R1.4.1b, link only);
  `disableSideloadFlags` (📖 R1.4.2); version floor covering the plugin-pin fix of 2.1.179 (📖 R6.2.7).
- **MCP:** `allowedMcpServers` with `allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true` (📖 R1.3.1, R1.3.4); match by
  `serverUrl` or `serverCommand` (exact argv), never `serverName`, which "is not a security control"
  (📖 R1.3.3); `disableClaudeAiConnectors: true` (📖 R1.3.7).
- **Review checklist** [design]: publisher, local or remote, what it reads and where it sends data,
  supplier-register entry and BAA/DPA status, no token passthrough (📖 R6.4.2), pinned version.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** Compliance gets an asset inventory and supplier records (P4c); unknown servers are
  refused before they load.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** waiting time for new tools; review effort for 1–2 DevSecOps people.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** `disableSideloadFlags` does not cover `.mcp.json` or `claude mcp add`
  (📖 R1.4.2), so the MCP allowlist must be locked. No per-group targeting in server-managed settings
  (📖 R1.1.6). Tool description changes after approval are not covered (⚠️). Without MDM, laptops can
  bypass server-managed settings (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ G11). Evidence: OTel `plugin_installed` /
  `plugin_loaded` (📖 R1.4.6).
- **Next steps:** catalogue v1 in phase 1 (may slip to phase 2 only with owner agreement).

## 6. References

- Framework layer 4; layer 8 rollout.
- Related: ADR-0007.

# ADR-0007: Claude Code managed settings are hygiene, not the security boundary

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (D1, D3; OD4, OD7b, OD12)
- **Scope:** Claude Code on laptops (server-managed settings, Team plan) and in CI

## 1. Context

The brief names "permission prompts turned off" as a problem. It is tempting to make Claude Code
settings the main control. But server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not a security
boundary" (📖 R1.1.7), local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8), Bash rules are not a boundary
(📖 R1.2.6), and on laptops without MDM another login or provider skips server-managed settings
(📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ G11).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Settings as the boundary (lock everything, block auto mode) | Simple story | Bypassable on laptops; high friction; people work around it |
| B. Settings as hygiene; IAM and the CI gate as the boundary | Boundary holds even if settings are bypassed | Settings give weaker guarantees than they appear to |

## 3. Decision

Option B. The boundary is IAM (ADR-0002) and the merge gate (ADR-0003). Managed settings set safe,
uniform defaults:

- `permissions.defaultMode` = Manual, with a read-only allowlist that excludes `aws`, `pulumi`,
  `serverless` (D1, OD7b); auto mode stays available and is measured.
- `disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable"` (📖 R1.2.2); `requiredMinimumVersion` floor (📖 R1.1.13).
- Sandbox with `~/.aws` hidden; `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` kept `true` (OD12, 📖 R5.5.5b).
- `--restricted` in CI and in the incident-analysis session (D3; flag 📖 R6.9.1b).
- OTel exporter without prompt content (📖 R1.1.20).

Phase 1 ships `defaultMode`, the allowlist, bypass removal, the catalogue keys, the version floor and
OTel; the rest of the baseline follows in phase 2 (OD4).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** a bypassed or misconfigured agent still cannot write prod or read PHI. Compliance gets
  one organization policy with evidence instead of personal choices.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** more prompts than auto mode; a prompt for every `aws` read. S5
  ("nobody can turn off all prompts unnoticed") is likely unreachable without MDM (⚠️).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** the auto-mode classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions
  (📖 R6.3.5); fallback to `disableAutoMode` if the planted-injection test steers it (D1). The live
  settings are edited in the admin console, not by PR (📖 R1.1.5); an Owner exports them monthly and
  diffs them with git until a better method exists (G18).
- **Next steps:** phase-1 subset; planted-injection test in phase 3.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 2; layer 8 rollout; research 6.6 (D1–D3).
- Related: ADR-0002, ADR-0006.

# ADR-0008: CI uses OIDC; no long-lived CI keys, with one time-boxed exception

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (S2; OD1, OD6)
- **Scope:** GitHub Actions deploy workflows to AWS, GCP, k0s and Firebase

## 1. Context

CI becomes the only routine production writer (ADR-0001), so it is the main target. Repository
secrets can be read by anyone with write access (📖 R3.5.3b), which includes every engineer and their
agent. A long-lived key there is standing prod write in disguise.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Keep stored keys, rotate them | No migration | Standing prod write for all writers |
| B. OIDC everywhere, no exception | S2 = 0 | k0s and Firebase may not support it yet (G1, G2) |
| C. OIDC for AWS and GCP; a controlled exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials | Removes most keys now | One exception to manage |

## 3. Decision

Option C.

- **AWS:** GitHub OIDC (📖 R3.4.1); the prod role trusts only the `production` environment of the
  monorepo (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4), ideally narrowed by `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
- **GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization (📖 R3.4.5b).
- **k0s/Firebase exception** (OD1, OD6): CI deploy credentials only, until it is checked whether they
  can use OIDC. Conditions [design]: a `production` environment secret, never a repository secret
  (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3); GitHub-hosted runners, because on self-hosted runners environment secrets act
  like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5); a single source of truth; owner, expiry, rotation.
- `GITHUB_TOKEN` default "restricted" (📖 R3.5.3); actions pinned by lockfile or full SHA (📖 R3.5.5).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** no stored AWS or GCP keys to leak (S2); every deploy credential is tied to a reviewed
  workflow on `main`.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** one-time migration; slower action updates. The exception remains until
  G1/G2 are solved.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can change or delete the environment, and a deleted
  environment comes back without protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); alerts and a settings comparison cover it.
  The GitHub Apps used for CI agents and the required check have their own keys (⚠️ G19).
  Runtime credentials inside the cluster are out of the exception (OD6).
- **Next steps:** OIDC and removal of stored keys in phase 1; k0s/Firebase credentials moved to
  environment secrets before standing prod write is removed.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 1 ("CI → AWS", "CI → GCP"), layer 5 ("Credentials").
- Related: ADR-0001.

# ADR-0009: The coding agent stays outside PHI; real-data reads are approved per tenant

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (research 1.9; GĐ-9, GĐ-14)
- **Scope:** coding-agent sessions on laptops and in CI; production stores of all insurer tenants

## 1. Context

Papaya holds medical records, national IDs and bank accounts for several insurer tenants in
different countries. Claude Team is not shown as BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Partner-uploaded claim
documents are both PHI and a prompt-injection vector (research 1.11.4 L6). Neither OWASP nor NIST
knows a full prevention for prompt injection (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Agent reads prod data freely | Fastest debugging | PHI in transcripts; injection can exfiltrate; no BAA |
| B. Agent never reads any customer data | Simplest rule | Blocks legitimate debugging of non-PHI data |
| C. Agent outside PHI; other personal data case by case under an approved, per-tenant grant | Matches the owner's boundary; debugging still possible | Process controls on some paths |

## 3. Decision

Option C.

- **PHI:** never in an agent session. A human reads in a terminal without an agent and gives the
  agent a redacted summary. A store that holds PHI counts as PHI unless the agent reads a view without
  it [design].
- **Other personal data:** readable within an approved request naming one tenant, purpose, store,
  window and agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9); data-read role, 1 h [design]. At night the
  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day [design].
- **Partner documents:** reproduced with synthetic documents or de-identified first [design].
- **Non-prod:** synthetic or masked only (GĐ-14); no prod copies (S11).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM for AWS stores; one record per
  exception (S9). Assumes injection succeeds and limits what it can reach.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** debugging with redacted or synthetic data; a request for each real read.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** of the 17 paths to PHI (research 1.11.4), tickets, chat, pasted text,
  admin pages and CI logs are covered by process only. Per-tenant scoping through session tags is
  unresolved (⚠️ R2.1.8). Data-plane deny actions are incomplete (⚠️ G13). Planted-injection test in
  phase 3.
- **Next steps:** non-prod data scan and the minimal real-data read flow in phase 1; data-plane SCP in
  phase 2.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 6; layer 1 (SCPs); research 1.9, 1.11.4, 5.8.
- Related: ADR-0002, ADR-0006.

- **Next steps:** non-prod data scan and the minimal real-data read flow in phase 1; data-plane SCP in

# ADR-0001: Every production change goes through a reviewed PR applied by CI

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9, "A + D2'")
- **Scope:** all writes to production AWS, k0s and Firebase; incidents included

## 1. Context

Engineering wants Claude Code to talk to AWS directly; Compliance wants no production change without
a named human who reviewed and approved it. Today engineers can deploy from laptops (GĐ-10,
unconfirmed), so an agent on that laptop can deploy too. Incidents are where the pressure to bypass
review is highest.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. PR → approval → CI deploy for everything ("IaC first") | One path, approval before apply, evidence by construction | Slower incidents (est. 11–46 min ⚠️ vs 2–20 min, Options §6) |
| B. SSM Automation runbooks with an approval step | Approval inside AWS | Not verified that it meets the approval rule (G6); only for operations someone scripted |
| C. JIT direct access for the engineer + agent | Fastest | Approves access, not the change; agent holds prod write |
| D. Hosted agent with its own identity | Clean separation | New platform; does not remove the need for approval |

## 3. Decision

Option A is the default path for every production change, incidents included. A narrow JIT
fallback exists only when the PR path cannot be used during an incident (ADR-0005). The owner accepts
that this fallback meets the approval rule only partly (Options §9 Q2). Incident target: ≤ 30 min from
decision to apply.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** the PR, its approvals, the run log and CloudTrail form one evidence chain keyed by
  commit SHA. Agent-written and human-written changes pass the same checks (S10).
- **Negative / trade-offs:** slower incident fixes; operations that are not in IaC must first be
  written as code or a runbook. Two write paths remain (PR and JIT), while the framing asked for one.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** the fallback stays narrow only if most incidents are expressible in
  IaC (unknown, Options §8). Metrics: JIT grants per month, share of incidents needing non-IaC
  operations; above about 25 %, make the PR lane faster or add a runbook, never widen JIT.
- **Next steps:** measure the incident PR lane on one service first (phase 1).

## 6. References

- Framework §1 and layer 3; `work/03-options.md` §1, §6, §9.
- Related: ADR-0002, ADR-0003, ADR-0005.

# ADR-0002: Nobody holds standing prod write; the agent's identity is read-only metadata

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9; D2)
- **Scope:** AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets and SCPs on the prod OU; k0s and GCP by the same principle

## 1. Context

On a laptop the agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and one portal session reaches every role
assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate "agent"
permission set therefore does not separate the agent from the engineer (⚠️ R2.9 #1). Whatever the
engineer holds, the agent holds.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Separate agent permission set, engineer keeps write | Looks like least privilege | Same SSO cache: the agent can still assume the write role |
| B. No standing prod write for anyone; `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role | Agent cannot write prod with the engineer's identity | Engineers also lose direct writes and raw-log reads |
| C. Separate OS user or container for agent sessions | Real separation of credentials | More setup; planned for phase 3 only |

## 3. Decision

Option B. Prod is written only by the CI pipeline role, or by an approved, time-boxed JIT grant
(ADR-0005). The standing prod role is `ProdReadMetadata` [design name]: metrics, redacted log groups,
configuration of services whose secrets are resolved at runtime; no data-plane reads of claim stores;
1-hour role session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). SCPs on the prod OU deny data-plane reads and direct
Lambda updates except for named roles (pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4, R4.6 #3). Option C follows in phase 3.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** an agent, even a manipulated one, cannot write prod or read customer data with the
  engineer's standing identity. Compliance gets least privilege enforced by IAM (S1).
- **Negative / trade-offs:** during the transition, engineers lose raw logs and configuration of
  services not yet redacted; they need a data-read grant in an incident. Process rules remain where
  IAM cannot separate engineer and agent: no agent in the JIT terminal (D2).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** SSO-token theft during a session could open later grants (⚠️);
  mitigations are a short portal session and a fresh sign-in before a grant. The data-plane action
  list is incomplete (⚠️ G13). Identity Center assignment export is reviewed quarterly.
- **Next steps:** phase 1 removes broad read roles only after the minimal real-data read flow works,
  then removes standing prod write once its prerequisites are in place.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 1, layer 2 ("Trade-off on AWS credentials"), layer 8 rollout.
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0005, ADR-0009.

# ADR-0003: The merge to `main` is the approval gate: two people, code owners, on-call co-ownership

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-5, GĐ-8, GĐ-11; OD2, OD5, OD7, OD9, OD10, OD13)
- **Scope:** GitHub monorepo rulesets, CODEOWNERS, `production` environment, on-call schedule

## 1. Context

On GitHub Team, environment required reviewers do not exist for private repositories (📖 R3.1.2), so
the deploy job cannot wait for an approval. The approval must happen earlier. Incidents need an
approver within 15 minutes, 24/7 (S7), and code-owner review means the approver must own the files.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Upgrade to Enterprise for environment reviewers | Approval sits next to the deploy | Cost; not assumed (GĐ-5) |
| B. Merge to `main` as the gate; `production` limited to `main` | Works on Team; the approver sees the code that will be applied | Nobody sees the prod diff before apply (handled by ADR-0004) |
| C. More approvers for high-risk changes | More eyes | Slower; the owner wants two people per change |

## 3. Decision

Option B. Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, empty
bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). `production` accepts only `main` (📖 R3.1.3).

- **Two people per change:** one makes it, one approves it; the approver is always an engineer,
  never an agent (OD2, OD5). L3 changes need one approver too, who must own the path.
- **Incidents:** on-call engineers only approve; an incident responder writes the fix (OD7).
- **Night coverage:** an on-call approver group co-owns every deployable path in CODEOWNERS; one
  primary, one backup (OD9). It does not co-own process-defining paths (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS,
  agent config, catalogue) or the SCP stack, which only the L3 owner team approves (OD13).
- **Cross-team PRs:** one approval is enough (OD10).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** four-eyes enforced by GitHub, not by the agent. One rule for normal days and incidents.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** GitHub accepts an approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so the
  on-call group can approve another domain's PR; domain review on normal days is a process rule.
  One reviewer for high-risk changes can miss things (owner's trade-off for speed).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can edit the gate (logged, not prevented, 📖 R3.2.2);
  alerts on ruleset changes and a monthly report of cross-domain approvals on PRs without the
  `incident` label. An agent could approve through its engineer's login; no detection found (⚠️).
- **Next steps:** rulesets, CODEOWNERS and its validation check in phase 1; the composition of the L3
  owner team is open (G17).

## 6. References

- Framework layer 3 ("Gate = merge to `main`", "Who approves at night"), layer 7 (audit alerts).
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004.

# ADR-0004: Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until a stack owner approves the prod preview

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (OD8, OD11, OD13)
- **Scope:** deploy workflows for Pulumi and Serverless stacks; k0s and Firebase not covered yet

## 1. Context

With the gate at merge time (ADR-0003), the approver reviews the code change, not the prod diff. A
PR may not preview prod, because that would run PR code with state-write and secret access
(📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). So a stateful delete or an IAM change can reach prod without anyone
seeing its real effect. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files such as
`serverless.yml`, not in separate L3 paths.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Accept the gap | No extra step | Destructive diffs applied unseen |
| B. Risk stop, approved by the L3 owner team | Specialist review | Often a third person; L3 team must be on call 24/7 |
| C. Risk stop, approved by an owner of the stack | Stays at two people; works at night | Less specialist review; compensated by automated checks |

## 3. Decision

Option C [design]. The deploy job on `main` previews prod. On stateful replace/delete, an IAM
change, a network or security-group change, or (from phase 2) an advisory policy finding, it stops
and posts the filtered preview. The original author opens a PR adding
`deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml` with the SHA and preview hash; the first approver approves it
(OD13). If that approver is unavailable, another stack owner approves; this makes three people and
is recorded as a deviation (OD11). After the merge the workflow previews again on the new HEAD and
continues only if the hash matches. Serverless uses `serverless diff --json`, parsed by CI because
differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2). A `mandatory` Pulumi policy violation always
blocks `pulumi up` (📖 R4.2.2).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** the person who approves now sees the prod diff for the changes that can do lasting
  damage. Still two people in the normal case.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** a stopped stack blocks later merges to it, including an incident fix,
  until the approval lands or the change is reverted. One more review round when the stop fires.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** preview output may not be stable enough to hash (⚠️ Options §8); if
  not, compare a structured summary. Until phase 2, the risk stop is the only compensation for OD8;
  Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and policy packs follow. k0s and Firebase have no
  preview step in this design (⚠️ G1, G2).
- **Next steps:** risk stop in the deploy job in phase 1.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 3 ("Risk stop"), layer 5 (required checks); `work/03-options.md` §1.
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0003.

# ADR-0005: Break-glass is a time-limited, approved JIT grant, for incidents only

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (Options §9 Q2; D2; OD7, OD13)
- **Scope:** AWS production accounts through IAM Identity Center; k0s and Firebase not covered (G1, G2)

## 1. Context

Some incidents cannot use the PR path: GitHub or Actions is down, the pipeline is broken, or the
operation is not in IaC and has no runbook. Without a defined fallback, people keep standing access
"just in case", which ADR-0002 removes.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. No fallback | Single path | Outage of GitHub blocks every fix; pressure to keep standing access |
| B. Standing break-glass account | Always available | Standing prod write; hard to audit |
| C. Approved JIT grant, 1-hour role session, command list, reconciled after | Approval before use; time-boxed; traceable | Approves a command list, not an applied change (partial) |

## 3. Decision

Option C, used only during an incident when the PR path cannot be used.

- **Request:** command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub.
- **Approval:** the on-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant; the on-call approver counts as
  owner of the service (OD13).
- **Grant:** `InfraOperator-<service>` [design name], assigned via `CreateAccountAssignment` and removed
  via `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2); role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4).
- **Execution:** the incident responder types the commands in a terminal without an agent (D2, OD7).
- **After:** CloudTrail writes in the window are compared with the list; a codify PR follows by a
  fixed deadline; drift detection runs until it merges.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** no standing prod write even for emergencies; every use has an approval, a window and
  a reconciliation.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** meets the approval rule only partly (owner accepted). "No agent in the
  JIT terminal" is a process rule: the grant is reachable from the same laptop.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** deleting the assignment likely stops only new sessions, so a grant
  can run up to about 2 h (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3). An immediate stop needs the revocation SCP, which keeps
  the user blocked ≥ 12 h (📖 R2.4.4); no night-time path to apply it is designed yet (⚠️ G20).
  Metrics: JIT used where a PR was possible, writes outside the list, late codify PRs (review at 1).
- **Next steps:** minimal JIT with per-grant CloudTrail comparison in phase 1; revocation SCP and
  automated reconciliation in phase 2.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 7 ("Break-glass = JIT fallback"); `work/03-options.md` §4b, §9.
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0002.

# ADR-0006: MCP servers and plugins are allowed only from a reviewed, pinned catalogue

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (framing Q8; OD4)
- **Scope:** Claude Code on all engineer laptops and in CI; Papaya's internal plugin marketplace

## 1. Context

Local MCP servers, plugins and hooks run with the engineer's access (📖 R1.6.2, R5.5.5); remote MCP
servers receive tokens and data. Papaya already runs an internal plugin marketplace and uses MCP for
Linear and Slack. An unreviewed server or a plugin update can read the repo, the SSO cache or claim
data and send it out.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Free choice, guidance only | No friction | No inventory; any server can exfiltrate |
| B. Denylist known-bad servers | Low friction | Misses new and changed servers |
| C. Allowlist (catalogue) enforced by managed settings | Inventory and supplier records; blocks unknown servers | Up to 5 working days' wait for a new tool (S6) |

## 3. Decision

Option C. The catalogue is a file in git, changed by PR under the L3 owner team.

- **Plugins:** only Papaya's marketplace via managed `strictKnownMarketplaces`, plus
  `blockedMarketplaces` (📖 R1.4.2); sources pinned to `ref`/`sha` (📖 R1.4.1b, link only);
  `disableSideloadFlags` (📖 R1.4.2); version floor covering the plugin-pin fix of 2.1.179 (📖 R6.2.7).
- **MCP:** `allowedMcpServers` with `allowManagedMcpServersOnly: true` (📖 R1.3.1, R1.3.4); match by
  `serverUrl` or `serverCommand` (exact argv), never `serverName`, which "is not a security control"
  (📖 R1.3.3); `disableClaudeAiConnectors: true` (📖 R1.3.7).
- **Review checklist** [design]: publisher, local or remote, what it reads and where it sends data,
  supplier-register entry and BAA/DPA status, no token passthrough (📖 R6.4.2), pinned version.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** Compliance gets an asset inventory and supplier records (P4c); unknown servers are
  refused before they load.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** waiting time for new tools; review effort for 1–2 DevSecOps people.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** `disableSideloadFlags` does not cover `.mcp.json` or `claude mcp add`
  (📖 R1.4.2), so the MCP allowlist must be locked. No per-group targeting in server-managed settings
  (📖 R1.1.6). Tool description changes after approval are not covered (⚠️). Without MDM, laptops can
  bypass server-managed settings (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ G11). Evidence: OTel `plugin_installed` /
  `plugin_loaded` (📖 R1.4.6).
- **Next steps:** catalogue v1 in phase 1 (may slip to phase 2 only with owner agreement).

## 6. References

- Framework layer 4; layer 8 rollout.
- Related: ADR-0007.

# ADR-0007: Claude Code managed settings are hygiene, not the security boundary

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (D1, D3; OD4, OD7b, OD12)
- **Scope:** Claude Code on laptops (server-managed settings, Team plan) and in CI

## 1. Context

The brief names "permission prompts turned off" as a problem. It is tempting to make Claude Code
settings the main control. But server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not a security
boundary" (📖 R1.1.7), local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8), Bash rules are not a boundary
(📖 R1.2.6), and on laptops without MDM another login or provider skips server-managed settings
(📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ G11).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Settings as the boundary (lock everything, block auto mode) | Simple story | Bypassable on laptops; high friction; people work around it |
| B. Settings as hygiene; IAM and the CI gate as the boundary | Boundary holds even if settings are bypassed | Settings give weaker guarantees than they appear to |

## 3. Decision

Option B. The boundary is IAM (ADR-0002) and the merge gate (ADR-0003). Managed settings set safe,
uniform defaults:

- `permissions.defaultMode` = Manual, with a read-only allowlist that excludes `aws`, `pulumi`,
  `serverless` (D1, OD7b); auto mode stays available and is measured.
- `disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable"` (📖 R1.2.2); `requiredMinimumVersion` floor (📖 R1.1.13).
- Sandbox with `~/.aws` hidden; `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` kept `true` (OD12, 📖 R5.5.5b).
- `--restricted` in CI and in the incident-analysis session (D3; flag 📖 R6.9.1b).
- OTel exporter without prompt content (📖 R1.1.20).

Phase 1 ships `defaultMode`, the allowlist, bypass removal, the catalogue keys, the version floor and
OTel; the rest of the baseline follows in phase 2 (OD4).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** a bypassed or misconfigured agent still cannot write prod or read PHI. Compliance gets
  one organization policy with evidence instead of personal choices.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** more prompts than auto mode; a prompt for every `aws` read. S5
  ("nobody can turn off all prompts unnoticed") is likely unreachable without MDM (⚠️).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** the auto-mode classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions
  (📖 R6.3.5); fallback to `disableAutoMode` if the planted-injection test steers it (D1). The live
  settings are edited in the admin console, not by PR (📖 R1.1.5); an Owner exports them monthly and
  diffs them with git until a better method exists (G18).
- **Next steps:** phase-1 subset; planted-injection test in phase 3.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 2; layer 8 rollout; research 6.6 (D1–D3).
- Related: ADR-0002, ADR-0006.

# ADR-0008: CI uses OIDC; no long-lived CI keys, with one time-boxed exception

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (S2; OD1, OD6)
- **Scope:** GitHub Actions deploy workflows to AWS, GCP, k0s and Firebase

## 1. Context

CI becomes the only routine production writer (ADR-0001), so it is the main target. Repository
secrets can be read by anyone with write access (📖 R3.5.3b), which includes every engineer and their
agent. A long-lived key there is standing prod write in disguise.

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Keep stored keys, rotate them | No migration | Standing prod write for all writers |
| B. OIDC everywhere, no exception | S2 = 0 | k0s and Firebase may not support it yet (G1, G2) |
| C. OIDC for AWS and GCP; a controlled exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials | Removes most keys now | One exception to manage |

## 3. Decision

Option C.

- **AWS:** GitHub OIDC (📖 R3.4.1); the prod role trusts only the `production` environment of the
  monorepo (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4), ideally narrowed by `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
- **GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization (📖 R3.4.5b).
- **k0s/Firebase exception** (OD1, OD6): CI deploy credentials only, until it is checked whether they
  can use OIDC. Conditions [design]: a `production` environment secret, never a repository secret
  (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3); GitHub-hosted runners, because on self-hosted runners environment secrets act
  like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5); a single source of truth; owner, expiry, rotation.
- `GITHUB_TOKEN` default "restricted" (📖 R3.5.3); actions pinned by lockfile or full SHA (📖 R3.5.5).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** no stored AWS or GCP keys to leak (S2); every deploy credential is tied to a reviewed
  workflow on `main`.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** one-time migration; slower action updates. The exception remains until
  G1/G2 are solved.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can change or delete the environment, and a deleted
  environment comes back without protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); alerts and a settings comparison cover it.
  The GitHub Apps used for CI agents and the required check have their own keys (⚠️ G19).
  Runtime credentials inside the cluster are out of the exception (OD6).
- **Next steps:** OIDC and removal of stored keys in phase 1; k0s/Firebase credentials moved to
  environment secrets before standing prod write is removed.

## 6. References

# ADR-0009: The coding agent stays outside PHI; real-data reads are approved per tenant

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (research 1.9; GĐ-9, GĐ-14)
- **Scope:** coding-agent sessions on laptops and in CI; production stores of all insurer tenants

## 1. Context

Papaya holds medical records, national IDs and bank accounts for several insurer tenants in
different countries. Claude Team is not shown as BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Partner-uploaded claim
documents are both PHI and a prompt-injection vector (research 1.11.4 L6). Neither OWASP nor NIST
knows a full prevention for prompt injection (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Agent reads prod data freely | Fastest debugging | PHI in transcripts; injection can exfiltrate; no BAA |
| B. Agent never reads any customer data | Simplest rule | Blocks legitimate debugging of non-PHI data |
| C. Agent outside PHI; other personal data case by case under an approved, per-tenant grant | Matches the owner's boundary; debugging still possible | Process controls on some paths |

## 3. Decision

Option C.

- **PHI:** never in an agent session. A human reads in a terminal without an agent and gives the
  agent a redacted summary. A store that holds PHI counts as PHI unless the agent reads a view without
  it [design].
- **Other personal data:** readable within an approved request naming one tenant, purpose, store,
  window and agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9); data-read role, 1 h [design]. At night the
  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day [design].
- **Partner documents:** reproduced with synthetic documents or de-identified first [design].
- **Non-prod:** synthetic or masked only (GĐ-14); no prod copies (S11).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM for AWS stores; one record per
  exception (S9). Assumes injection succeeds and limits what it can reach.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** debugging with redacted or synthetic data; a request for each real read.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** of the 17 paths to PHI (research 1.11.4), tickets, chat, pasted text,
  admin pages and CI logs are covered by process only. Per-tenant scoping through session tags is
  unresolved (⚠️ R2.1.8). Data-plane deny actions are incomplete (⚠️ G13). Planted-injection test in
  phase 3.
- **Next steps:** non-prod data scan and the minimal real-data read flow in phase 1; data-plane SCP in
  phase 2.

## 6. References

- Framework layer 6; layer 1 (SCPs); research 1.9, 1.11.4, 5.8.
- Related: ADR-0002, ADR-0006.

  - "non-prod L1 không cần duyệt", tức vòng lặp non-prod tự do. Đây là thứ chính Engineering nhận được;
  - OD3 (`CLAUDE.md` và agent config là L3). Không ADR nào trích OD3.
  ADR-0003 và 0004 chỉ chạm tới một phần. Lớp evidence chain/audit (change record, đối chiếu hàng tháng, drift; layer 7) cũng không có ADR. Tôi coi đây là thiếu nhỏ hơn và chấp nhận được nếu README nói rõ.
- Sửa: thêm ADR-0010 "Risk level decides who approves; non-prod needs none" (L0–L3, OD2, OD3, GĐ-14). Hoặc ít nhất ghi trong README rằng mô hình risk level và audit chain chỉ nằm trong framework.

**M5. Yêu cầu "with examples" của owner hầu như chưa được đáp ứng.**
- Vị trí: hầu hết các ADR. Ngoại lệ: 0004 có đường dẫn `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml`.
- Vấn đề: framework có sẵn các ví dụ cụ thể nhưng ADR không dùng: sự cố Lambda lúc 2 giờ sáng (layer 3), mẫu yêu cầu JIT "INC-123 ... `aws ecs update-service ...`" (layer 7, ⚠️ illustrative).
- Sửa: thêm 1–2 dòng ví dụ:
  - 0001 hoặc 0003: Lambda timeout 30→90 s qua PR `incident`, R duyệt, khoảng 11–46 phút ⚠️;

1. **ADR-0003 dòng 42:** "admins can edit the gate (logged, not prevented, 📖 R3.2.2)". Framework tách rõ: phần logging là 📖 R3.2.2, còn việc admin sửa được là ⚠️ R3.2.2, R3.6 #1. Sửa marker cho đúng như vậy.
2. **ADR-0001 dòng 39:** "above about 25 %". Ngưỡng này là ⚠️ (framework: "starting thresholds ⚠️ to calibrate, a value new in this draft"). Thêm ⚠️.

4. **ADR-0001 Scope dòng 6:** ghi "all writes to production AWS, k0s and Firebase" nhưng không nói k0s/Firebase không có fallback khi Actions ngừng và không có risk stop (G1, G2). GCP cũng không được nhắc. Thêm một câu, hoặc trỏ tới ADR-0005 Scope.

6. **ADR-0002 Decision dòng 28–29:** SCPs được ghi mà không có mốc phase. Framework: data-plane deny và Lambda update deny thuộc phase 2. Thêm "(phase 2)".
7. **ADR-0002 Negative dòng 35–36:** "they need a data-read grant in an incident" có thể hiểu là kể cả configuration. Framework: configuration lấy từ IaC code, chỉ raw log mới cần grant L3-data. Nên làm rõ.
8. **ADR-0003 Options B, dòng 20:** "(handled by ADR-0004)" là nói quá. Risk stop chỉ bắt diff rủi ro của Pulumi/Serverless. Đổi thành "partly handled".
9. **ADR-0004 Negative dòng 40:** "blocks later merges to it". Framework hiểu là các *deploy* của merge sau bị dừng (vì hash khác), còn merge vẫn diễn ra. Sửa thành "later deploys to that stack stop".

# ADR-0010: Risk level decides who approves, not how many; non-prod needs no approval

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-14; OD2, OD3, OD8, OD9)
- **Scope:** every change made by engineers and their agents, from non-prod to production

## 1. Context

Engineering's ask is speed: let the agent read, change and deploy freely. Compliance's sentence is
about production writes only (framing §3.1). A single rule for all changes either slows non-prod for
no gain or leaves high-risk prod changes with too light a review. The owner also wants every prod
change to need exactly two people: one who makes it and one who approves it (OD2).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Same approval for everything | Simple | Non-prod loop slowed for no gain; high-risk changes get no extra scrutiny |
| B. More approvers as risk grows (e.g. two for L3) | More eyes on dangerous changes | Breaks the two-person rule; slower incidents |
| C. Risk level narrows who may approve, plus a risk stop; non-prod free | Fast where damage is small; specialist owners where it is large | One reviewer for high-risk changes can miss things |

## 3. Decision

Option C [design levels]:

| Level | What | Approval |
|---|---|---|
| L0 | Reads: non-prod anything, prod metadata | none |
| L1 | Changes in non-prod (synthetic or masked data only, GĐ-14) | none, author only |
| L2 | Routine prod change, e.g. Lambda memory 1024 → 2048 MB | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher |
| L3 | IAM/SCP, stateful replace/delete, network, workflow and agent-config files | 1 owner of that path; IaC changes also meet the risk stop (ADR-0004) |
| L3-JIT | Break-glass in an incident | on-call approver ≠ requester (ADR-0005) |
| L3-data | Real customer data read | approver ≠ requester + agreement (ADR-0009) |

`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent-configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for the
whole team (OD3). Process-defining paths and the SCP stack are owned by the L3 owner team; IAM or
stateful changes inside a domain file are approved by that stack's owners (OD8, OD13).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** a free non-prod loop for engineers and agents (S4); the same two-person rule for every
  prod change, incidents included. Compliance gets a written rule for who may approve what.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** one approver for high-risk changes (owner's trade-off for speed);
  `CLAUDE.md` edits wait for the L3 owner team, not the domain team that edits them most.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** the free loop holds only if non-prod has no real data; a non-prod
  store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule until scanned (S11). A risky diff hidden in an L2 PR is
  caught by the risk stop, not by the level.

# ADR-0010: Risk level decides who approves, not how many; non-prod needs no approval

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-14; OD2, OD3, OD8, OD9)
- **Scope:** every change made by engineers and their agents, from non-prod to production

## 1. Context

Engineering's ask is speed: let the agent read, change and deploy freely. Compliance's sentence is
about production writes only (framing §3.1). A single rule for all changes either slows non-prod for
no gain or leaves high-risk prod changes with too light a review. The owner also wants every prod
change to need exactly two people: one who makes it and one who approves it (OD2).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Same approval for everything | Simple | Non-prod loop slowed for no gain; high-risk changes get no extra scrutiny |
| B. More approvers as risk grows (e.g. two for L3) | More eyes on dangerous changes | Breaks the two-person rule; slower incidents |
| C. Risk level narrows who may approve, plus a risk stop; non-prod free | Fast where damage is small; specialist owners where it is large | One reviewer for high-risk changes can miss things |

## 3. Decision

Option C [design levels]:

| Level | What | Approval |
|---|---|---|
| L0 | Reads: non-prod anything, prod metadata | none |
| L1 | Changes in non-prod (synthetic or masked data only, GĐ-14) | none, author only |
| L2 | Routine prod change, e.g. Lambda memory 1024 → 2048 MB | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher |
| L3 | IAM/SCP, stateful replace/delete, network, workflow and agent-config files | 1 owner of that path; IaC changes also meet the risk stop (ADR-0004) |
| L3-JIT | Break-glass in an incident | on-call approver ≠ requester (ADR-0005) |
| L3-data | Real customer data read | approver ≠ requester + agreement (ADR-0009) |

`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent-configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for the
whole team (OD3). Process-defining paths and the SCP stack are owned by the L3 owner team; IAM or
stateful changes inside a domain file are approved by that stack's owners (OD8, OD13).

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** a free non-prod loop for engineers and agents (S4); the same two-person rule for every
  prod change, incidents included. Compliance gets a written rule for who may approve what.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** one approver for high-risk changes (owner's trade-off for speed);
  `CLAUDE.md` edits wait for the L3 owner team, not the domain team that edits them most.
- **Risks & how we watch them:** the free loop holds only if non-prod has no real data; a non-prod
  store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule until scanned (S11). A risky diff hidden in an L2 PR is
  caught by the risk stop, not by the level.
- **Next steps:** non-prod data scan and CODEOWNERS with the L3 path list in phase 1; composition of
  the L3 owner team is open (G17).

## 5. References

- Framework layer 3 (levels table), layer 5 (canonical L3 path list), layer 6 (non-prod).
- Related: ADR-0003, ADR-0004, ADR-0005, ADR-0009.
